blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ XXIV
AUTOMORPHISMS OF REDUCTIVE GROUPSby M. Demazure

The first part of this exposé (nos 1 to 5) is a direct consequence of the existence, for a reductive group, of "sufficiently many outer automorphisms", a result which is itself a consequence of the weakest form of the isomorphism theorem for pinned groups. The second part (nos 6 and 7) presents two applications of the more precise results of the preceding exposé; in particular, no 7 uses the theorem on generators and relations in its explicit form. Finally, we have given in an appendix (no 8) some results of "Galois" cohomology used in the text.

Let us make our cohomological notation precise: if \(S\) is a prescheme and \(G\) an \(S\)-group prescheme, we shall denote by \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\) the first cohomology set of \(S\) with coefficients in \(G\), computed for the (fpqc) topology; it is also the set of isomorphism classes of principal homogeneous (fpqc) sheaves under \(G\). We shall denote by \(\mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S, G)\) the corresponding set for the étale topology; it is thus the part of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\) formed by the classes of homogeneous sheaves under \(G\) which are quasi-isotrivial (= locally trivial for the étale topology). We shall denote by \(\operatorname{Fib}(S, G)\) the part of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\) formed by the classes of representable sheaves (principal homogeneous bundles). We thus have the inclusions \[ \begin{gathered} \mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S, G) \subset \mathrm{H}^1(S, G),\\ \operatorname{Fib}(S, G) \subset \mathrm{H}^1(S, G). \end{gathered} \] If every principal homogeneous sheaf under \(G\) is representable (for example if \(G\) is quasi-affine over \(S\), cf. SGA VIII 7.9), we thus have \(\operatorname{Fib}(S, G) = \mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\).

If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism for the (fpqc) topology, we denote by \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G)\) the kernel of the canonical map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G) \to \mathrm{H}^1(S', G_{S'})\). It is known that \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G)\) can be computed simplicially (TDTE II, § A.4), which implies that when \(S' \to S\) is covering for the étale topology, it is also the kernel of \(\mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S, G) \to \mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S', G_{S'})\).

Finally, we call "theorem 90" the following assertion: "every principal homogeneous sheaf under \(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}\) is representable and locally trivial." (Exp. VIII, 4.5), an assertion equivalent to "\(\mathrm{H}^1(S, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) = \operatorname{Pic}(S)\)", or again to "\(\mathrm{H}^1(S, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) = 0\) for \(S\) local (resp. semi-local)".

pages.title: 1. Scheme of automorphisms of a reductive group

blocks.html: 1. Scheme of automorphisms of a reductive group

It is appropriate first to make certain definitions of the preceding exposé precise. Let \(S\) be a non-empty prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R^*, R_0)\) a pinned reduced root datum. We call a pinning of \(G\) of type \(\mathscr{R}\), or an \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinning of \(G\), the datum of:

(i) an isomorphism of \(\mathrm{D}_S(M)\) onto a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) (or, what amounts to the same thing, a monomorphism \(\mathrm{D}_S(M) \to G\) whose image is a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\)), identifying \(R\) with a root system of \(G\) relative to \(T\) (Exp. XIX, 3.6) and \(R^*\) with the set of corresponding coroots,
(ii) for each \(\alpha \in R_0\), an \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^\alpha)^*\).
In order for \(G\) to possess an \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinning, it is necessary and sufficient that it be splittable and of type \(\mathscr{R}\) (Exp. XXII, 2.7).

If \(u : G \to G'\) is an isomorphism of \(S\)-reductive groups, to every \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinning \(\mathscr{E}\) of \(G\) there corresponds, by "transport of structure", an \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinning \(u(\mathscr{E})\) of \(G'\). If \(v : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) is an isomorphism of pinned root data, to every \(\mathscr{R}'\)-pinning \(\mathscr{E}\) of \(G'\) there corresponds, by transport of structure, an \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinning \(v(\mathscr{E})\) of \(G'\).

Let us call a pinned group a triple \((G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) where \(G\) is an \(S\)-reductive group, \(\mathscr{R}\) a pinned reduced root datum, and \(\mathscr{E}\) a pinning of \(G\) of type \(\mathscr{R}\). We call an isomorphism of the pinned group \((G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) onto the pinned group \((G', \mathscr{R}', \mathscr{E}')\) a pair \((u, v)\) where \(u\) is an isomorphism \(u : G \to G'\) and \(v\) an isomorphism of pinned root data \(v : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\), such that \(u(\mathscr{E}) = v(\mathscr{E}')\).

N. B. If \(S\) is non-empty, \(v\) is uniquely determined by \(u\), and we shall also say, by abuse of language, that \(u\) is an isomorphism of the pinned groups. In particular, if \((G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) is a pinned group, an automorphism of \((G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) is therefore an automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) such that there exists an automorphism \(v\) of \(\mathscr{R}\) with \(u(\mathscr{E}) = v(\mathscr{E})\); it is thus an automorphism of \(G\) which normalises \(T\), induces on \(T\) an automorphism of the form \(\mathrm{D}_S(h)\), where \(h\) is an automorphism of \(M\), and permutes among themselves the elements \(X_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\). (As one sees easily, the preceding conditions do in fact characterise the automorphisms of \((G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\)).

We have an obvious contravariant functor \[ \Phi : \quad (G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E}) \mapsto \mathscr{R}, \qquad (u, v) \mapsto v \] and the main result of the preceding exposé (Exp. XXIII, 4.1) shows us that it is a fully faithful functor (we shall see moreover in the following exposé that it is an equivalence of categories). It follows in particular that the group of automorphisms of \((G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) is canonically isomorphic to the group of automorphisms of the pinned root datum \(\mathscr{R}\) (cf. Exp. XXIII, 5.5).

Let \(S\) be a prescheme; let us endow \((\mathbf{Sch})_{/S}\) with the (fpqc) topology and consider the \(S\)-group sheaf \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\), where \(G\) is an \(S\)-group prescheme. We have an exact sequence of \(S\)-group sheaves \[ 1 \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G) \longrightarrow G \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{int}\ } \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \] which defines a monomorphism \[ j : G/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G). \] The image sheaf of \(j\) is the sheaf of inner automorphisms of \(G\); in order for an automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) to be inner, it is necessary and sufficient that there exist a covering family \(\{S_i \to S\}\) and, for each \(i\), a \(g_i \in G(S_i)\) such that \(\operatorname{int}(g_i) = u_{S_i}\). If \(v\) is another automorphism of \(G\), one sees at once that \(\operatorname{int}(v)u = vuv^{-1}\) is the inner automorphism defined by the family \(g'_i = v(g_i)\). It follows that the image of \(j\) is normal in \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\). The quotient group sheaf, denoted \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\), is the sheaf of outer automorphisms of \(G\). We thus have an exact sequence \[ 1 \longrightarrow G/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow 1. \] The preceding definitions are all compatible with base change. They are of course valid in any site.

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \((G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) a pinned \(S\)-reductive group. Let \(E\) be the (abstract) group of automorphisms of the pinned root datum \(\mathscr{R}\), i.e. the group of automorphisms of \(\mathscr{R}\) normalising \(R_0\). By Exp. XXIII, 5.5, we have a canonical monomorphism \[ E \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \] which associates with \(h \in E\) the unique automorphism of the pinned group \(G\) such that \(\Phi(u) = h\). This monomorphism canonically defines a monomorphism of sheaves \[ a : \quad E_S \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G). \] In order for an automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) to be a section of the image sheaf of \(a\), it is necessary and sufficient that the following conditions be satisfied:

(i) \(u\) normalises \(T\). One then knows that \(u\) permutes the roots of \(G\) relative to \(T\). If \(\alpha \in R\), then \(u(\alpha) : t \mapsto \alpha(u^{-1}(t))\) is therefore, locally on \(S\), of the form \(t \mapsto \beta(t)\), \(\beta \in R\). The second condition is then written as follows:

(ii) If \(\alpha \in R_0\) and if \(U\) is an open subset of \(S\) such that \(u(\alpha)_U \in R\), then \(u(\alpha)_U \in R_0\) and one has \[ \operatorname{Lie}(u_U)(X_\alpha)_U = (X_{u(\alpha)})_U. \]
It follows at once from the definitions that the sections of \(a(E_S)\) normalise the subgroups of \(G\) defined by the pinning: \(T\), \(B\), \(B^-\), \(U\), \(U^-\).
These definitions being laid down, we have:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. Consider the canonical exact sequence of \(S\)-group sheaves \[ 1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{ad}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow 1. \]

(i) \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\) is representable by a smooth and separated \(S\)-prescheme.

(ii) \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) is representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-prescheme with finite generation (Exp. X, 5.1).

(iii) If \(G\) is splittable, the preceding exact sequence is split. More precisely, for every pinning of \(G\), the morphism (cf. 1.2) \[ p \circ a : \quad E_S \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \] is an isomorphism.
Let us first show how the theorem is deduced from:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.4

In the notation of 1.2, \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\) is the semi-direct product \(a(E_S) \cdot \operatorname{int}(G)\).

The lemma implies the theorem at once when \(G\) is splittable. Since \(G\) is locally splittable for the étale topology (Exp. XXII, 2.3), hence also for the (fppf) topology, and since the latter is "of effective descent" for the fibred category of twisted constant morphisms (Exp. X, 5.5), one deduces (ii) in the general case (cf. Exp. IV, 4.6.8). To deduce (i) from it, one notes that \(\operatorname{int}(G) \simeq \operatorname{ad}(G)\) is affine over \(S\), so that the morphism \(p\) is affine when \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\) is representable, and one concludes by descent of affine schemes.
It therefore only remains for us to prove 1.4. For this, it suffices to prove:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.5

If \((\mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) and \((\mathscr{R}', \mathscr{E}')\) are two pinnings of the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\), there exists a unique inner automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) over \(S\) transforming one pinning into the other (i.e. such that there exists \(v : \mathscr{R}' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathscr{R}\) with \(u(\mathscr{E}) = v(\mathscr{E}')\), cf. 1.0).
1.5.1. Uniqueness. —

It suffices to prove that if \(G\) is a pinned \(S\)-group and if \(\operatorname{int}(g)\) is an automorphism of pinned group (\(g \in G(S)\)), then \(\operatorname{int}(g) = \mathrm{id}\). Now one has first \(\operatorname{int}(g)T = T\), \(\operatorname{int}(g)B = B\), hence \(g \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T)(S) \cap \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(B)(S) = T(S)\) (cf. for example Exp. XXII, 5.6.1). It follows that \(\operatorname{int}(g)\) normalises each \(U_\alpha\) and that \[ \operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{int}(g)) X_\alpha = \operatorname{Ad}(g) X_\alpha = \alpha(g)\, X_\alpha \] for \(\alpha \in R_0\). One therefore has \(\alpha(g) = 1\) for \(\alpha \in R_0\), hence \(g \in \bigcap_{\alpha \in R_0} (\operatorname{Ker} \alpha)(S) = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G)(S)\) (Exp. XXII, 4.1.8). Q.E.D.
1.5.2. Existence. —

It suffices to prove it locally for the (fpqc) topology. Let \[ (T, M, R, R_0, (X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R_0}) \quad \text{and} \quad (T', M', R', R'_0, (X'_{\alpha'})_{\alpha' \in R'_0}) \] be the two pinnings. By conjugacy of maximal tori, we may assume \(T = T'\). After possibly restricting \(S\), we may assume that the isomorphism \(\mathrm{D}_S(M) \simeq \mathrm{D}_S(M')\) comes from an isomorphism \(M \simeq M'\) carrying \(R\) onto \(R'\), and we are reduced to the situation \(T = T'\), \(M = M'\), \(R = R'\). Since the systems of simple roots are conjugate under the Weyl group (Exp. XXI, 3.3.7), we may likewise assume \(R_0 = R'_0\). There then exists, for each \(\alpha \in R_0\), a scalar \(z_\alpha \in \mathbf{G}_m(S)\) such that \(X'_\alpha = z_\alpha X_\alpha\), and it suffices to construct, locally for (fpqc), a section \(t\) of \(T\) such that \(\alpha(t) = z_\alpha\) for each \(\alpha \in R_0\). But the morphism \(T \to (\mathbf{G}_{m,S})^{R_0}\) with components \(\{\alpha,\ \alpha \in R_0\}\) is the dual of an injection \(\mathbf{Z}^{R_0} \to M\), hence is faithfully flat, which completes the proof of 1.5.2 and therefore of 1.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.6

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\) is affine (resp. of finite type, resp. of finite presentation, resp. quasi-compact) over \(S\).

(ii) \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) is finite over \(S\).

(iii) For every \(s \in S\), one has \(\operatorname{rgred}(G_s) - \operatorname{rgss}(G_s) \leqslant 1\).
Indeed, since \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\) is affine, flat and of finite presentation over \(S\), the morphism \(p\) is affine, faithfully flat and of finite presentation.

If \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) is finite over \(S\), it is affine over \(S\), hence so is \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\), which proves (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). If \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\) is quasi-compact over \(S\), it is of finite presentation over \(S\) (being in any case locally of finite presentation and separated over \(S\)); by Exp. V, 9.1, \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) is then of finite presentation over \(S\), hence finite, which proves (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii). Finally, to prove the equivalence of (ii) and (iii), we may assume \(G\) split, and we are reduced to Exp. XXI, 6.7.8.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.7

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. Then \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)^0 = \operatorname{int}(G) \simeq \operatorname{ad}(G)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.8

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) an \(S\)-group prescheme which is smooth, affine and with connected fibres over \(S\). Then the \(S\)-functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \] is representable by a smooth and separated \(S\)-prescheme (which is affine over \(S\) if \(G\) is semi-simple).

Indeed, let \(U\) be the set of points \(t\) of \(S\) such that \(H_t\) is reductive; it is open (Exp. XIX, 2.6); if \(S'\) is an \(S\)-prescheme, \(H_{S'}\) is reductive if and only if \(S' \to S\) factors through \(U\). It follows that the canonical morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \to S\) factors through \(U\). We may therefore assume \(S = U\), and we are reduced to:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two \(S\)-reductive groups. Then \[ F = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G') \] is representable by a smooth and separated \(S\)-prescheme (affine if \(G\) or \(G'\) is semi-simple). Moreover, \(S\) decomposes into a sum of two open sub-preschemes \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) such that \(F_{S_1} = \varnothing\) and such that \(F_{S_2}\) is a left (resp. right) principal homogeneous bundle under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S_2\text{-gr.}}(G'_{S_2})\) (resp. \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S_2\text{-gr.}}(G_{S_2})\)).
Indeed, let \(S_2\) be the set of points of \(S\) where \(G\) and \(G'\) are of the same type, and let \(S_1\) be its complement.

Since the type of a reductive group is a locally constant function, \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are open. It is clear that \(F_{S_1} = \varnothing\), and we may assume \(S = S_2\). By Exp. XXIII, 5.6, \(F\) is a principal homogeneous sheaf under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\), locally trivial for the étale topology. It follows that \(F_0 = F/\operatorname{ad}(G)\) is a principal homogeneous sheaf under \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\), locally trivial for the étale topology, hence representable (Exp. X, 5.5). Since \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\) is affine, \(F\) is therefore also representable.
Let us note that in the course of the proof we have obtained:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.10

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two \(S\)-reductive groups of the same type at each \(s \in S\). Then \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\) operates freely (on the right) on \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\), the quotient sheaf \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G') = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')/\operatorname{ad}(G) \] is representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-prescheme, which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) (and which is therefore finite over \(S\) if \(G\) is semi-simple). Moreover, the isomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G') \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G', G) \] defined by \(u \mapsto u^{-1}\) induces an isomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G') \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G', G). \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.11

If \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')(S) \ne \varnothing\), one says that \(G\) is an inner twisted form of \(G'\); then \(G'\) is an inner twisted form of \(G\); one may then reduce the structure group of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\) to \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\). More precisely, let \(u \in \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')(S)\), regarded as a section \(u : S \to \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')\). Let us denote by \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}_u(G, G') \] the inverse image, under the canonical morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G') \to \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')\), of the closed sub-prescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')\) which is the image of \(u\). The natural operation of \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\) on \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}_u(G, G')\) endows this prescheme with a structure of principal homogeneous bundle; by extension of the structure group \(\operatorname{ad}(G) \to \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}_u(G, G')\) gives back \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\).
By Hensel's lemma (Exp. XI, 1.11), 1.8 yields at once:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.12

Let \(S\) be a henselian local scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(G'\) a smooth affine \(S\)-group with connected fibres, \(s\) the closed point of \(S\). If \(G_s\) and \(G'_s\) are isomorphic algebraic \(k(s)\)-groups, then \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic. More precisely, every \(k(s)\)-isomorphism \(G_s \simeq G'_s\) comes from an \(S\)-isomorphism \(G \simeq G'\).
Applying now 1.7 (resp. 1.12) to the scheme of dual numbers over a field, we obtain, by Exp. III, 2.10 (resp. 3.1):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.13

Let \(k\) be a field and \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group. Then \[ \mathrm{H}^1(G, \operatorname{Lie}(G/k)) = \mathrm{H}^2(G, \operatorname{Lie}(G/k)) = 0. \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.14

(i) The assertion concerning \(\mathrm{H}^1\) was known (CHEVALLEY); that concerning \(\mathrm{H}^2\) was proved in most of the cases of the classification by CHEVALLEY.

(ii) In fact, the conjunction of 1.13 and of the uniqueness theorem over an algebraically closed field is essentially equivalent to the uniqueness theorem. A direct proof of 1.13 would therefore give a way of deducing the general uniqueness theorem from CHEVALLEY's uniqueness theorem over a field.

The existence of reductive groups of all types over all preschemes (Exp. XXV) shows that the obstructions to lifting a reductive \(k\)-group \(G\) over the artinian rings with residue field \(k\) (which by Exp. III, 3.8 are elements of \(\mathrm{H}^3(G, \operatorname{Lie}(G/k)) \otimes V\)) where \(V\) is a certain \(k\)-vector space) vanish. This seems to suggest that \(\mathrm{H}^3(G, \operatorname{Lie}(G/k)) = 0\). Here again, a direct proof of this fact (if it is true) would doubtless give a way of deducing the general existence theorem from the existence theorem over a field (Chevalley's Tôhoku).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.15

Let \(k\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group. Regard \(k\) as a trivial \(G\)-module. Then \[ \mathrm{H}^1(G, k) = \mathrm{H}^2(G, k) = 0. \]

Consider indeed the reductive \(k\)-group \(H = G \times_k \mathbf{G}_{m,k}\). One has \(\operatorname{Lie}(H/k) = \operatorname{Lie}(G/k) \oplus k\), a decomposition stable under \(H\). For an arbitrary \(H\)-Module \(M\), one has \(\mathrm{H}^i(H, M) = \mathrm{H}^i(G, \mathrm{H}^0(\mathbf{G}_{m,k}, M))\) (this follows from the characterisation of the \(\mathrm{H}^i(H, -)\) as derived functors of \(\mathrm{H}^0(H, -) = \mathrm{H}^0(G, \mathrm{H}^0(\mathbf{G}_{m,k}, -))\), and from the fact that the functor \(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathbf{G}_{m,k}, -)\) is exact, cf. Exp. I, no 5). In particular, one has \[ \mathrm{H}^i(H, \operatorname{Lie}(H/k)) = \mathrm{H}^i(G, \operatorname{Lie}(G/k)) \oplus \mathrm{H}^i(G, k) \quad \text{for } i > 0. \] One then concludes by applying 1.13 to the reductive group \(H\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.16

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. We call a form of \(G\) over \(S\) an \(S\)-group prescheme \(G'\) locally isomorphic to \(G\) for (fpqc) (it amounts to the same to say (cf. Exp. XXIII, 5.6) that \(G'\) is locally isomorphic to \(G\) for (ét), or again that \(G'\) is an \(S\)-reductive group of the same type as \(G\) at each point of \(S\)).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.17

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. The functor \[ G' \longmapsto \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G') \] is an equivalence between the category of forms of \(G\) over \(S\) and the category of principal homogeneous bundles under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\).

If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism, forms of \(G\) trivialised by \(S'\) and bundles trivialised by \(S'\) correspond to one another. Every principal homogeneous sheaf under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\) is representable and quasi-isotrivial (locally trivial for the étale topology).

The first assertion is formal in the category of sheaves (for (fpqc), say). On the other hand, every sheaf locally isomorphic to \(G\) (for (fpqc)) is representable (since \(G\) is affine over \(S\)) and locally isomorphic to \(G\) for (ét). Finally, for every form \(G'\) of \(G\), the \(S\)-sheaf \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\) is representable (1.8). The corollary follows at once.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.18

The set of isomorphism classes of forms of the reductive group \(G\) over \(S\) is isomorphic to \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)) = \mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S, \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)) = \operatorname{Fib}(S, \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)). \] If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism, the subset formed by the forms trivialised by \(S'\) is isomorphic to \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G))\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.19

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \(\mathscr{R}\) a pinned reduced root datum such that \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\) exists (a condition automatically satisfied, Exp. XXV). Let us write \[ \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}) = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})) = \operatorname{ad}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})) \cdot E(\mathscr{R})_S. \]

(i) The set of isomorphism classes of \(S\)-reductive groups of type \(\mathscr{R}\) (Exp. XXII, 2.7, cf. Exp. XXIII, 5.12) is isomorphic to \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})) = \mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S, \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})) = \operatorname{Fib}(S, \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})). \]

(ii) If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism, the subset formed by the classes of groups splittable over \(S'\) is isomorphic to \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}))\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.20

With the preceding notation, with every \(S\)-reductive group of type \(\mathscr{R}\) there is canonically associated a right principal homogeneous bundle under \(\underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})\): \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}), G) = P. \] Let us note that \(P\) is to be interpreted as the "scheme of pinnings of \(G\) of type \(\mathscr{R}\)" (cf. 1.0). Moreover, \(P\) is likewise a (left) principal homogeneous bundle under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\), a structure which appears at once in the description above.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.21

Let \(S\) be a henselian local scheme, \(s\) its closed point. The functor \[ G \longmapsto G_s \] induces a bijection from the classification of \(S\)-reductive groups onto that of \(k(s)\)-reductive groups.

In particular, for every \(S\)-reductive group \(G\), there exists a finite surjective étale morphism \(S' \to S\) such that \(G_{S'}\) is splittable.

Using the existence of the \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\) (Exp. XXV), we are reduced to proving that, if we write \(H = \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})\), the canonical map \[ \operatorname{Fib}(S, H) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Fib}(k(s), H_s) \] is bijective (and that every element of \(\operatorname{Fib}(S, H)\) has the property indicated above). Now every finite subset of \(H\) is contained in an affine open set (this is indeed trivial for a constant group, and \(H\) is affine over a constant group); we may therefore use the result proved in the appendix (8.1).
2. Automorphisms and subgroups

Let us introduce a notation: if \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\), and if \(X\) is a subfunctor of \(G\), we write \[ \begin{aligned} \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, X) &= \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_H(X),\\ \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, \mathrm{id}_X) &= \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_H(X). \end{aligned} \] One defines similarly \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, X, Y)\), …, \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, X; G', X')\), ….

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\) (resp. \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\), resp. \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\)). Let \(T^{\mathrm{ad}}\) (resp. \(B^{\mathrm{ad}}\)) denote the maximal torus (resp. the Borel group) of \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\) corresponding to \(T\) (resp. \(B\)): \[ \begin{aligned} B^{\mathrm{ad}} &\simeq B/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G) = B/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(B),\\ T^{\mathrm{ad}} &\simeq T/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G). \end{aligned} \] Then \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)\) (resp. \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B)\), resp. \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T)\)) is representable by a closed subprescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\), smooth over \(S\), and the exact sequence of 1.3 induces an exact sequence \[ e \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}}) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow e \] (resp. \[ e \longrightarrow B^{\mathrm{ad}} \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow e, \] resp. \[ e \longrightarrow T^{\mathrm{ad}} \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow e). \]

By descent of closed subpreschemes, one is at once reduced to the case where \(G\) is pinned and where \(B \supset T\) is its canonical Killing couple (cf. Exp. XXII, 5.5.5 (iv)). Since the group \(E\) of 1.2 normalizes \(B\) and \(T\), the result follows at once from the normalization theorems in \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\) (Exp. XXII, 5.3.12 and 5.6.1).
Using now the conjugacy theorems (cf. Exp. XXIII, 5.12), and reasoning as in no 1, we deduce:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two reductive \(S\)-groups of the same type at each point. Let \(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) be a Killing couple of \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)).

(i) The \(S\)-functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T; G', T')\) is representable by a smooth closed subprescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\) which is principal homogeneous under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)\).

Moreover, \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}})\) acts freely on this prescheme, and one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T; G', T')/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}}) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G'). \]

(ii) The \(S\)-functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B; G', B')\) is representable by a smooth closed subprescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\) which is principal homogeneous under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B)\).

Moreover, \(B^{\mathrm{ad}}\) acts freely on this prescheme and one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B; G', B')/B^{\mathrm{ad}} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G'). \]

(iii) The \(S\)-functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T; G', B', T')\) is representable by a smooth closed subprescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\) which is principal homogeneous under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T)\).

Moreover, \(T^{\mathrm{ad}}\) acts freely on this prescheme and one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T; G', B', T')/T^{\mathrm{ad}} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G'). \]
Reasoning again as in no 1, we deduce:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\). The functor \[ (G', T') \longmapsto \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T; G', T'), \] resp. \[ (G', B') \longmapsto \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B; B', B'), \] resp. \[ (G', B', T') \longmapsto \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T; G', B', T'), \] is an equivalence between the category of couples \((G', T')\) (resp. of couples \((G', B')\), resp. of triples \((G', B', T')\)), where \(G'\) is a form of \(G\) and \(T'\) a maximal torus of \(G'\) (resp. \(B'\) a Borel group of \(G'\), resp. \(B' \supset T'\) a Killing couple of \(G'\)), and the category of principal homogeneous bundles under the \(S\)-group \(H\), where \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)\) (resp. \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B)\), resp. \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T)\)).

Moreover, every principal homogeneous sheaf under \(H\) is representable and quasi-isotrivial, so that one has \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, H) = \mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S, H) = \operatorname{Fib}(S, H). \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.4

Under the conditions of 2.2, the morphism written set-theoretically as \(u \mapsto u(T)\) (resp. \(u \mapsto u(B)\), resp. \(u \mapsto (u(B), u(T))\)) induces an isomorphism \[ \begin{aligned} \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')/\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T) &\simeq \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G')\\ \text{resp.}\quad \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')/\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B) &\simeq \underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(G'),\\ \text{resp.}\quad \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')/\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T) &\simeq \underline{\mathrm{Kil}}(G'). \end{aligned} \] The proof is immediate: it suffices to carry it out locally for (fpqc), so we may suppose \(G \simeq G'\), and we are reduced to Exp. XXII, 5.8.3 (iii).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.5

The preceding results are at once interpreted in terms of restriction of the structural group: if \(G'\) is a form of \(G\), corresponding to the principal bundle \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\), to give a restriction of the structural group of this bundle to \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)\) amounts to giving a maximal torus \(T'\) of \(G'\), the bijections suggested above being that of 2.4 on the one hand, and the map \(T' \mapsto \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T; G', T')\) on the other. Similarly for Borel groups and Killing couples.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6

Under the conditions of corollary 2.2 (i), \(T^{\mathrm{ad}}\) acts freely on \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T; G', T')\), the quotient \[ P = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T; G', T')/T^{\mathrm{ad}} \] is representable; it is a principal homogeneous bundle under \[ \mathrm{A} = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)/T^{\mathrm{ad}}, \] where \(\mathrm{A}\) is representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-prescheme, an extension of \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) by \(W_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}}) = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}})/T^{\mathrm{ad}}\). Moreover, if one lets \(\mathrm{A}\) act on \(T\) in the evident way, the bundle associated with \(P\) is none other than \(T'\).

The first part of the proposition follows at once from the preceding results. To prove the second, one observes that there is an evident morphism \(P \times_S T \to T'\) (defined by \((u, t) \mapsto u(t)\)); to show that after passage to the quotient by \(\mathrm{A}\) it induces an isomorphism, one may once again suppose \((G, T) \simeq (G', T')\), in which case this is immediate.
In an entirely similar manner, one has:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.7

Under the conditions of corollary 2.2 (ii), if one lets \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T)/T^{\mathrm{ad}} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) act on \(T\) in the evident way, the bundle associated with \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')\) is none other than \(T'\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.8

Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two reductive \(S\)-groups which are inner twisted forms of one another; let \(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) be a Killing couple of \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)). Then \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.9

It is not true in general that \(B\) and \(B'\) are isomorphic; they are however inner twisted forms of one another (cf. no 5).
One can develop "\(\underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}\)" variants of the preceding results. Let us point out one of them:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.10

Under the conditions of 2.2 (iii), let \(u \in \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')(S)\); consider \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}_u(G, B, T; G', B', T') = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T; G', B', T') \cap \underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}_u(G, G'). \] This is a smooth affine \(S\)-prescheme which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(T^{\mathrm{ad}}\). In particular, \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}_u(G, B, T; G', B', T')(S) \ne \varnothing\) if and only if the corresponding element of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, T^{\mathrm{ad}})\) is zero.
To conclude this no, let us prove two results which will be useful to us in what follows:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.11

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). The evident morphism \[ T^{\mathrm{ad}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, \mathrm{id}_T) \] is an isomorphism.
This follows from the preceding statements; moreover, a direct proof was given in the course of the proof of 1.5.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.12

Under the preceding conditions, there exists an equivalence between the category of couples \((G', f)\), where \(G'\) is a form of \(G\) and \(f\) an isomorphism of \(T\) onto a maximal torus of \(G'\), and the category of principal homogeneous bundles under \(T^{\mathrm{ad}}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.13

If \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, T^{\mathrm{ad}}) = 0\), and if \(G'\) is a form of \(G\) possessing a maximal torus isomorphic to \(T\), then \(G'\) is isomorphic to \(G\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.14

Let \(S\) be a prescheme such that \(\operatorname{Pic}(S) = 0\), and \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group of constant type. For \(G\) to be splittable, it is necessary and sufficient that \(G\) possess a trivial maximal torus.

Let \(G\) be a reductive group, \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) its radical (Exp. XXII, 4.3.9); since \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) is central and characteristic in \(G\), one has a canonical morphism \[ q : \quad \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{rad}(G)). \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.15

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. The following sequence is exact: \[ e \longrightarrow \operatorname{ad}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G;\ \text{id. on }\operatorname{rad}(G)) \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \xrightarrow{\ q\ } \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{rad}(G)). \] Moreover, \(\operatorname{Ker}(q) = \operatorname{Im}(p)\) is an open and closed subprescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\), finite over \(S\).
We may suppose \(G\) split. The first assertion is immediate; the second follows from Exp. XXI, 6.7.5 and 6.7.7.
Writing \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G,\ \text{id. on }\operatorname{rad}(G))\), we deduce:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.16

There exists an equivalence between the category of couples \((G', f)\), where \(G'\) is a form of \(G\) and \(f\) an isomorphism of \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) onto the radical of \(G'\), and the category of principal bundles under a certain \(S\)-group prescheme \(H\), where \(H\) is such that there exists an exact sequence \[ 1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{ad}(G) \longrightarrow H \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow 1, \] where the \(S\)-group \(F\) is étale and finite over \(S\).

pages.title: 3. Dynkin scheme of a reductive group. Quasi-split groups

blocks.html: 3. Dynkin scheme of a reductive group. Quasi-split groups

Recall (Exp. XXI, 7.4.1) that a Dynkin diagram is a finite set equipped with the structure defined by a set of couples of distinct elements (links) and by a map into \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) (lengths). To each reduced pinned root datum \(\mathscr{R}\) is associated a Dynkin diagram \(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{R})\), whose underlying set is the set of simple roots.

Let \(S\) be a prescheme. An \(S\)-Dynkin scheme is a finite twisted constant \(S\)-scheme \(\mathrm{D}\), equipped with the structure defined by a subscheme \(\mathrm{L}\) of \(\mathrm{D} \times_S \mathrm{D}\) whose intersection with the diagonal is empty, and by a morphism \(\mathrm{D} \to \{1, 2, 3\}_S\). For each \(S' \to S\), \(\mathrm{D}(S')\) is naturally equipped with a structure of Dynkin diagram.

One defines at once the following notions: isomorphism of two Dynkin schemes, base extension of a Dynkin scheme, constant Dynkin scheme associated with a Dynkin diagram. Every descent datum on a Dynkin scheme for the étale topology is effective.

We propose to associate with each reductive \(S\)-group \(G\) an \(S\)-Dynkin scheme. Suppose first that \(G\) is splittable over \(S\); for every pinning \(\mathscr{E}\) of \(G\), let \(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{E})\) denote the constant Dynkin scheme associated with the pinned root datum defined by \(\mathscr{E}\); if \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(\mathscr{E}'\) are two pinnings of \(G\), there exists by 1.5 a unique inner automorphism of \(G\) over \(S\) carrying \(\mathscr{E}\) into \(\mathscr{E}'\); this automorphism of \(G\) defines an isomorphism \(a_{\mathscr{E}\mathscr{E}'} : \mathrm{D}(\mathscr{E}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{D}(\mathscr{E}')\); the \(a_{\mathscr{E}\mathscr{E}'}\) evidently form a transitive system, so that one may identify the \(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{E})\) (i.e. take the inductive limit); the result is a constant Dynkin scheme denoted \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\). If now \(G\) is an arbitrary reductive \(S\)-group, there exists a covering family for the étale topology \(\{S_i \to S\}\) such that \(G_{S_i}\) is splittable. Reasoning as above, one thus has a canonical descent datum on the \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G_{S_i})\), which allows one to construct by descent an \(S\)-Dynkin scheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\).
This construction satisfies the following properties (which moreover characterize it essentially):

(i) To each reductive \(S\)-group is associated a Dynkin scheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\); to every isomorphism \(u : G \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } G'\) is functorially associated an isomorphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(u) : \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G')\).
(ii) If \(S'\) is an \(S\)-prescheme and \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, one has \[ \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G \times_S S') \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \times_S S'. \]
(iii) If \(\mathscr{E}\) is a pinning of \(G\), defining the pinned root datum with Dynkin diagram \(\mathrm{D}\), one has \[ \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \simeq \mathrm{D}_S. \]
(iv) If \(u\) is an inner automorphism of \(G\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(u)\) is the identity automorphism of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\).

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. It is clear that the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\) of automorphisms of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) for the Dynkin scheme structure is representable by a finite twisted constant \(S\)-scheme. By 3.4 (i) and (ii), one has a canonical morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)), \] which, in virtue of (iv), factors through a morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)). \] More generally, if \(G\) and \(G'\) are two reductive \(S\)-groups, one has a canonical morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G') \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G), \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G')); \] in particular, if \(G'\) is an inner twisted form of \(G\) (1.11), the Dynkin schemes \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G')\) are isomorphic.

If \(G\) is semi-simple (resp. adjoint or simply connected), the morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \] is a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism). Indeed, we may suppose \(G\) pinned, and we are reduced to the corresponding result for reduced pinned root data (cf. Exp. XXI, 7.4.5).

One has an analogous result for the \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}\); whence it follows in particular that two adjoint (resp. simply connected) semi-simple \(S\)-groups are inner twisted forms of one another if and only if their Dynkin schemes are isomorphic.

One may give a different construction of the Dynkin scheme associated with a reductive group. Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a reduced pinned root datum, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathscr{R}\); let \(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{R})\) denote the Dynkin diagram defined by the root datum \(\mathscr{R}\). One has (3.5) a canonical morphism \[ \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}) = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{R})_S). \] By corollary 1.17, the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\) corresponds to a principal homogeneous bundle \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}), G)\) under \(\underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})\). The associated bundle under \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{R})_S)\) corresponds to a form over \(S\) of \(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{R})_S\): it is \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\); in other terms, this associated bundle is none other than \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\mathrm{D}(\mathscr{R})_S, \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\). Under this last form, the proof is immediate.
3.8. Dynkin scheme and Killing couples. —

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\). There exists a canonical morphism \[ i : \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,S}) \] which identifies \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) with the "scheme of simple roots of \(B\) relative to \(T\)"; this morphism is defined at once by descent from the pinned case. Let us note moreover that the datum of \(T\) and of \(i\) allows one to reconstruct \(B\) ("one-to-one correspondence between systems of simple roots and systems of positive roots").

It follows from the preceding description of \(\mathfrak{D} = \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) that there exists a canonical root of \(B_{\mathfrak{D}}\) with respect to \(T_{\mathfrak{D}}\): this root \(\alpha_{\mathfrak{D}}\) is the image under \(i(\mathfrak{D})\) of the identity morphism of \(\mathfrak{D}\). One deduces from this a canonical invertible \(\mathscr{O}_{\mathfrak{D}}\)-Module \(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}}\): \[ \mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}} = (\mathfrak{g} \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_S} \mathscr{O}_{\mathfrak{D}})^{\alpha_{\mathfrak{D}}}. \] In the pinned case, one has \[ \mathfrak{D} = \coprod_{\alpha \in R_0} S_\alpha, \] where each \(S_\alpha\) is a copy of \(S\), and \(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}}\) is the \(\mathscr{O}_{\mathfrak{D}}\)-Module which induces \(\mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) on \(S_\alpha\), for every \(\alpha \in R_0\).
3.9. Quasi-pinnings. Quasi-pinned groups. —
If \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group, one calls a quasi-pinning of \(G\) the datum of:
(i) a Killing couple \(B \supset T\) of \(G\),
(ii) a section \(X \in \Gamma(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G), \mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}})^*\).
A reductive \(S\)-group is said to be quasi-splittable if it possesses a quasi-pinning. By a quasi-pinned group one means a reductive group equipped with a quasi-pinning.

If \(B \supset T\) is a Killing couple of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\), then \(G\) is quasi-pinnable relative to this Killing couple if and only if \(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}}\) possesses a section that is non-zero at each point, i.e. if the element of \(\operatorname{Pic}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\) defined by \(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}}\) is zero. Suppose in particular that \(S\) is semi-local; then \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) is likewise semi-local, hence \(\operatorname{Pic}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) = 0\). Using in addition Exp. XXII, 5.9.7, we deduce:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.9.1

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. For \(G\) to be quasi-splittable, it is necessary and sufficient that it possess a Borel group.

Noting now that for an arbitrary reductive \(S\)-group the \(S\)-prescheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(G)\) is smooth and projective (Exp. XXII, 5.8.3), and hence possesses sections after a finite surjective étale extension of the base (EGA IV, § 24), we deduce the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.9.2

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. There exists an étale, finite and surjective morphism \(S' \to S\) such that \(G_{S'}\) is quasi-splittable.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.9.3

Under the preceding conditions, let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\) (cf. Exp. XIV, 3.20); then one may suppose moreover that \(G_{S'}\) is quasi-splittable relative to \(T_{S'}\): it suffices to apply the preceding reasoning to the "scheme of Borel groups containing \(T\)", which is finite and étale over \(S\) (Exp. XXII, 5.5.5 (ii)).

Let \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(\mathscr{E}'\) be two quasi-pinnings of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\). There exists a unique inner automorphism of \(G\) carrying \(\mathscr{E}\) into \(\mathscr{E}'\). Indeed, one is at once reduced to the split case, where the assertion has already been proved (1.5; it suffices in fact to note that, for an inner automorphism of \(G\), respecting a pinning or respecting the underlying quasi-pinning amount to the same thing). One concludes as in no 1 that a quasi-pinning of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\) defines a splitting \(h\) of the exact sequence: \[ 1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{ad}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \underset{p}{\overset{h}{\rightleftarrows}} \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \longrightarrow 1, \] the image of \(h\) being the subgroup of \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\) which leaves the quasi-pinning invariant.

Similarly, if \(G\) and \(G'\) are two quasi-pinned \(S\)-groups, one defines in a natural way the subfunctor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr. q-ép.}}(G, G') \] of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\); the projection of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G')\) onto \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')\) induces an isomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr. q-ép.}}(G, G') \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G'). \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.11

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(\mathscr{R}\) a reduced pinned root datum such that \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\) exists (cf. Exp. XXV), \(E\) the group of its automorphisms. Consider the three following categories:

(i) The category \(\underline{\mathrm{Rev}}\) of principal Galois coverings of \(S\) with group \(E\) (the morphisms are the isomorphisms).

(ii) The category \(\underline{\mathrm{Redext}}\) whose objects are the reductive \(S\)-groups of type \(\mathscr{R}\) (Exp. XXII, 2.7), the morphisms from \(G\) to \(G'\) being the elements of \(\underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')(S)\).

(iii) The category \(\underline{\mathrm{Q\acute{e}p}}\) of quasi-pinned reductive \(S\)-groups of type \(\mathscr{R}\) (the morphisms are the isomorphisms respecting the quasi-pinnings).

These three categories are equivalent: more precisely, one has a diagram of functors, commutative up to isomorphism \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Rev} \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{q\acute{e}p}} & & \mathrm{Q\acute{e}p} \ar[dl]^{i} \\ & \mathrm{Redext} \ar[ul]^{\mathrm{rev}} & } \] We shall describe these three functors below, leaving to the reader the task of verifying the commutativity of the diagram.
This is the obvious functor: \(i(G) = G\), \(i(f) =\) image of \(f\) under the morphism described in 3.10.
3.11.2. The functor qép. —

Let \(S'\) be a principal Galois covering of \(S\) with group \(E\). The canonical homomorphism \[ h : E \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}_{S'\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_{S'}(\mathscr{R})) = \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}(\mathscr{R})(S') \] defines an action of \(E\) on \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_{S'}(\mathscr{R})\), an action which respects the canonical quasi-pinning of \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\). Since \(S' \to S\) is covering for the (fpqc) topology, it is a morphism of effective descent for the fibred category of affine morphisms, and we denote by \[ \mathrm{q\acute{e}p}(S') = \mathrm{Q}\text{-}\mathrm{\acute{E}p}_{S'/S}(\mathscr{R}) \] the quasi-pinned \(S\)-group obtained by Galois descent.
3.11.3. The functor rev. —

Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathscr{R}\). We write \[ \operatorname{rev}(G) = \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}), G), \] this is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(E_S\) (cf. 1.10 and 1.19), that is to say an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Rev}}\).
Let us develop one of the corollaries of 3.11:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.12

For every reductive \(S\)-group \(G\), there exist a quasi-pinned \(S\)-group \(G_{\text{q-ép.}}\) and an "outer isomorphism" \(u \in \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G_{\text{q-ép.}}, G)(S)\). The pair \((G_{\text{q-ép.}}, u)\) is unique up to a unique isomorphism.
Indeed, we may assume \(G\) of constant type \(\mathscr{R}\), and we take \(G_{\text{q-ép.}} = \mathrm{Q}\text{-}\mathrm{\acute{E}p}_{\operatorname{rev}(G)/S}(\mathscr{R})\).

Let us note that the datum of the pair \((G_{\text{q-ép.}}, u)\) makes it possible to define canonically the \(S\)-prescheme (cf. 1.11) \[ \mathrm{Q} = \underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}(G_{\text{q-ép.}}, G), \] which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(\operatorname{ad}(G_{\text{q-ép.}})\), and the datum of which is "equivalent" to that of the inner twisted form \(G\) of \(G_{\text{q-ép.}}\). Moreover \(\mathrm{Q}\) is none other than the "scheme of quasi-pinnings of \(G\)", a definition which accounts for its structure of principal homogeneous bundle (on the left) under \(\operatorname{ad}(G)\) (3.10) – compare with 1.20.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.13

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an adjoint (resp. simply connected) semi-simple \(S\)-group, \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) the Dynkin \(S\)-scheme of \(G\). There exists a canonical isomorphism of \(S\)-preschemes in groups \[ T \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \prod_{\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)/S} \mathbf{G}_{m,\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)}\,. \]

(We recall (cf. Exp. II, § 1) that the right-hand side is by definition the \(S\)-functor which to \(S' \to S\) associates \(\mathbf{G}_m(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \times_S S')\), or, what amounts to the same thing, \(\mathbf{G}_m(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G_{S'}))\).)

First proof. Let us give it, for simplicity, in the adjoint case. Consider the composite morphism \[ T \longrightarrow \prod_{\mathfrak{D}/S} T_{\mathfrak{D}} \longrightarrow \prod_{\mathfrak{D}/S} \mathbf{G}_{m,\mathfrak{D}}\,, \] where the first morphism is the canonical morphism, the second is \(\prod_{\mathfrak{D}/S} \alpha_{\mathfrak{D}}\) (we have set \(\mathfrak{D} = \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\)). In order to verify that this morphism is an isomorphism, we may assume \(G\) split; but in that case it is none other than the morphism \(T \to (\mathbf{G}_{m,S})^{R_0}\) with components \(\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\), and this one is an isomorphism (Exp. XXII, 4.3.8).

Second proof. By 2.8, 3.5 and 3.11, we may assume that \(G = \mathrm{Q}\text{-}\mathrm{\acute{E}p}_{S'/S}(\mathscr{R})\), \(T\) being the canonical maximal torus. Over \(S'\), we have by Exp. XXII 4.3.8 an isomorphism \(T_{S'} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (\mathbf{G}_{m,S'})^{R_0}\), defined by the simple roots (resp. the simple coroots). The group \(E\) acts on the right-hand side by permutation of \(R_0\). Now the bundle associated with \(S'/S\) by \(E \to \operatorname{Aut}(R_0)\) is \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) (3.7), and we conclude at once.
Using 8.1, we deduce from this:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.14

Under the preceding conditions, we have \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, T) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{H}^1(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G), \mathbf{G}_m) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Pic}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)). \] In particular, \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, T) = 0\) when \(S\) is semi-local.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.15

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) a Killing couple of \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)), \(u \in \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, G')(S)\). Set (cf. 2.10) \[ P = \underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}_u(G, B, T; G', B', T'); \] this is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(T^{\mathrm{ad}}\) (by \((f, t) \mapsto f \circ \operatorname{int}(t)\)).

On the other hand, let \(\mathfrak{D} = \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) = \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G')\) (identified by means of \(u\) (3.5)), and let \(\mathrm{L} = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{\mathfrak{D}}(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}}, \mathfrak{g}'^{\mathfrak{D}})\) be the principal homogeneous bundle under \(\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathfrak{D}}\) defined by the invertible \(\mathscr{O}_{\mathfrak{D}}\)-Module \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{O}_{\mathfrak{D}}}(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}}, \mathfrak{g}'^{\mathfrak{D}}) = \mathfrak{g}'^{\mathfrak{D}} \otimes (\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}})^\vee. \]

Each \(f \in P(S')\) defines an isomorphism of \(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}} \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_S} \mathscr{O}_{S'}\) onto \(\mathfrak{g}'^{\mathfrak{D}} \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_S} \mathscr{O}_{S'}\), whence a canonical morphism \[ P \longrightarrow \prod_{\mathfrak{D}/S} \mathrm{L}\,. \] This morphism is an isomorphism, compatible with the isomorphism of operators \[ T^{\mathrm{ad}} \longrightarrow \prod_{\mathfrak{D}/S} \mathbf{G}_{m,\mathfrak{D}} \] defined above. Indeed, it suffices to verify this in the case where the two groups are pinned, where it is easy.

It follows in particular that under the isomorphism \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, T^{\mathrm{ad}}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Pic}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \] of 3.14, the class of the bundle \(P\) is carried into \(c\ell(\mathfrak{g}'^{\mathfrak{D}}) - c\ell(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}})\). The bundle \(P\) is therefore trivial if and only if \(\mathfrak{g}'^{\mathfrak{D}}\) and \(\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}}\) are isomorphic.

If \((G, B, T)\) is quasi-splittable, for instance if one takes for \(G\) the group \(G'_{\text{q-ép.}}\), with its canonical Killing couple, it follows that the image of the class of \(P\) is none other than the obstruction to the quasi-splitting of \(G'\) defined in 3.9.
3.16. Symmetries

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\). We recall (Exp. XXII, 5.9.1) that there exists a unique Borel group \(B^-\) of \(G\) such that \(B \cap B^- = T\). If \(X \in \Gamma(\mathfrak{D}, \mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}})^*\) defines a quasi-pinning of \(G\) relative to \((B, T)\) (3.9), then \(Y = -X^{-1} \in \Gamma(\mathfrak{D}, (\mathfrak{g}^{\mathfrak{D}})^\vee)^*\) defines a quasi-pinning of \(G\) relative to \((B^-, T)\); it is said to be the opposite quasi-pinning.

If \(\mathscr{R}\) is a reduced pinned root datum and if \(\mathscr{E}\) is an \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinning of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\), one defines an \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinning \(\mathscr{E}^-\), said to be opposite to \(\mathscr{E}\), in the following manner: one keeps the same maximal torus \(T\), one takes the opposite of the isomorphism \(\mathrm{D}_S(M) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } T\), and one "pins" by \(Y_\alpha = -X_\alpha^{-1} \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}^{-\alpha})^*\), for \(\alpha \in R_0\). The quasi-pinning underlying \(\mathscr{E}^-\) is the quasi-pinning opposite to the quasi-pinning underlying \(\mathscr{E}\).

Remark. — In the notation of Exp. XIX, 3.1, if one sets \[ w_\alpha(X_\alpha) = \exp(X_\alpha) \exp(-X_\alpha^{-1}) \exp(X_\alpha), \] one has \(w_\alpha(X_\alpha) = w_{-\alpha}(Y_\alpha)\) (loc. cit., 3.1 (vi)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.16.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group.

(i) Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\); there exists a unique \[ i_T \in \left(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)/T^{\mathrm{ad}}\right)(S) \subset \operatorname{Aut}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T) \] such that \(i_T(t) = t^{-1}\) for every section \(t\) of \(T\).

(ii) Let \((B, T)\) be a Killing couple of \(G\); there exists a unique section \[ w_{B,T} \in (\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T)/T)(S) = W_G(T)(S) \] such that \(\operatorname{int}(w_{B,T})(B) = B^-\) (with the obvious abuse of language).

(iii) Let \(\mathscr{Q} = (B, T, X)\) be a quasi-pinning of \(G\), \(\mathscr{Q}^- = (B^-, T, Y)\) the opposite quasi-pinning; there exists a unique inner automorphism of \(G\) \[ n_{\mathscr{Q}} \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}})(S) \subset \operatorname{Aut}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \] such that \(n_{\mathscr{Q}}(\mathscr{Q}) = \mathscr{Q}^-\), that is to say: \(n_{\mathscr{Q}}(T) = T\), \(n_{\mathscr{Q}}(B) = B^-\), \(n_{\mathscr{Q}}(X) = Y\).

(iv) Let \((\mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) be a pinning of \(G\), \((\mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E}^-)\) the opposite pinning; there exists a unique automorphism of \(G\) \[ u_{\mathscr{E}} \in \operatorname{Aut}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T) \subset \operatorname{Aut}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \] such that \(u_{\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{E}) = \mathscr{E}^-\), that is to say \(u_{\mathscr{E}}(t) = t^{-1}\) for every section \(t\) of \(T\), \(\operatorname{Ad}(u_{\mathscr{E}}) X_\alpha = Y_\alpha\) for \(\alpha \in R_0\).

Proof. (ii) follows from Exp. XXII, 5.5.5 (ii), then (iii) follows from 3.10, and (iv) follows from Exp. XXIII, 4.1. Finally, to prove (i), we may assume \(G\) pinned. The existence follows from (iv) for instance, the uniqueness from the fact that an automorphism of \(G\) inducing the identity on \(T\) is given by a section of \(T^{\mathrm{ad}}\) (2.11).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.16.3

We have \[ i_T^2 = w_{B,T}^2 = n_{\mathscr{Q}}^2 = u_{\mathscr{E}}^2 = e\,. \] Moreover, \(i_T\) (resp. \(u_{\mathscr{E}}\)) is \(\ne e\) if \(G \ne e\), and \(w_{B,T}\) (resp. \(n_{\mathscr{Q}}\)) is \(\ne e\) if \(G\) is not a torus.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.16.4

In the situation of (iii) (resp. (iv)), \(n_{\mathscr{Q}}\) projects onto \(w_{B,T}\) (resp. \(u_{\mathscr{E}}\) projects onto \(i_T\)) under the canonical morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}}) \longrightarrow W_{\operatorname{ad}(G)}(T^{\mathrm{ad}}) \simeq W_G(T)\,, \] resp. \[ \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)/T^{\mathrm{ad}}. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.16.5

The preceding definitions are compatible with base extension, and are functorial by isomorphism (in an obvious sense).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.16.6

(i) One can define in a unique manner, for each reductive group \(G\) over a prescheme \(S\), an element \[ s_G \in \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)(S) \] in such a way that this construction is functorial in \(G\) by isomorphism, is compatible with base changes, and that whenever \(T\) is a maximal torus of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\), \(s_G\) is the image of \(i_T\) under the canonical morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, T)/T^{\mathrm{ad}} \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G). \]

(ii) One has \(s_G^2 = e\), and \(s_G\) is a central element of \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\).

(iii) Under the conditions of 3.16.2 (ii), if one identifies \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B, T)/T^{\mathrm{ad}}\) with \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) (2.2), one has \[ w_{B,T}\, i_T = i_T\, w_{B,T} = s_G\,. \]

(iv) Under the conditions of 3.16.2 (iv), if one identifies \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S\text{-gr.-ép}}(G, \mathscr{R}, \mathscr{E})\) with \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\) (1.3 (iii)), one has \[ n_{\mathscr{E}}\, u_{\mathscr{E}} = u_{\mathscr{E}}\, n_{\mathscr{E}} = s_G\,. \]

Proof. (i) is proved without difficulty by descent. On the other hand, since \(i_T\) is obviously a central section of square \(e\) in \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T)\), (ii) follows immediately; (iii) is a consequence of (iv) by descent. Finally, under the conditions of (iv), it is clear that \(n_{\mathscr{E}} u_{\mathscr{E}} = u_{\mathscr{E}} n_{\mathscr{E}}\) and that this automorphism of \(G\) respects the pinning; modulo the identification made, it is therefore equal to its image in \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G)\); but \(n_{\mathscr{E}}\) is inner and \(u_{\mathscr{E}}\) projects onto \(s_G\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.16.7

(i) One determines \(a_G\) explicitly in each of the cases of the classification by means of (iii): it suffices, for each irreducible pinned root datum, to compose the symmetry with respect to the origin with the symmetry in the Weyl group (i.e. the element of the Weyl group such that \(w(R_0) = -R_0\)). One finds the following results: one has \(s_G = e\) except for \(\mathrm{A}_n\) (\(n \geqslant 2\)), \(\mathrm{D}_n\) (\(n\) odd) and \(\mathrm{E}_6\), in which case \(s_G\) is the unique non-trivial "outer automorphism".

(ii) The automorphism \(u_{\mathscr{E}}\) is the one which serves to construct "the compact real forms" in the theory of semi-simple Lie algebras.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.16.8

We defined in 3.16.1 an involution in the \(S\)-prescheme \(\mathrm{Q} = \underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}(G_{\text{q-ép.}}, G)\) of quasi-pinnings of \(G\) (cf. 3.12.1); by transport of structure from \(G_{\text{q-ép.}}\) to \(G\), one sees at once that this involution is given by the action of an element of \(\operatorname{ad}(G_{\text{q-ép.}})(S)\): the element \(n_0\) defined (3.16.2 (iii)) by the canonical quasi-pinning of \(G_{\text{q-ép.}}\).

In the same way, we have defined an involution in the \(S\)-prescheme \[ P = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}), G) \] of \(\mathscr{R}\)-pinnings of \(G\) (cf. 1.20). Reasoning as above, one sees that this involution is given by the action of the automorphism \(u_0\) of \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\) defined (3.16.2 (iv)) by the canonical pinning of \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\).

pages.title: 4. Isotriviality of reductive groups and of principal bundles under reductive groups

blocks.html: 4. Isotriviality of reductive groups and of principal bundles under reductive groups
4.1. Definitions. Isotriviality theorem

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-prescheme in groups, \(P\) a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\). One says that \(P\) is locally isotrivial (resp. semi-locally isotrivial) if for every point \(s \in S\) (resp. every finite set \(F\) of points of \(S\) contained in an affine open set) there exist an open set \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) (resp. \(F\)) and a finite surjective étale morphism \(S' \to U\) such that \(P_{S'}\) is trivial.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. One says that \(G\) is loc.isot. (resp. semi-loc.isot.) if for every point \(s \in S\) (resp. every finite set \(F\) of points of \(S\) contained in an affine open set) there exist an open set \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) (resp. \(F\)) and a finite surjective étale morphism \(S' \to U\) such that \(G_{S'}\) is splittable.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.1.3

(i) The equivalence of categories of 1.17 respects by definition local (resp. semi-local) isotriviality.

(ii) Let us add to the conditions of 4.1.1: \(G\) locally of finite presentation over \(S\). Then the principal bundle \(P\) (or the reductive group \(G\)) is locally isotrivial (resp. semi-locally isotrivial) if and only if for every \(S' \to S\), with \(S'\) local (resp. semi-local), \(P_{S'}\) is isotrivial (or \(G_{S'}\) isotrivial), that is to say if there exists \(S'' \to S'\) finite surjective étale such that \(P_{S''}\) is trivial (or \(G_{S''}\) split).

(iii) In the case of tori, definition 4.1.2 coincides with that of Exp. IX, 1.1.

Let us recall (Exp. XXII, 4.3 and 6.2) that for every reductive group \(G\) we have introduced the groups \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\), \(\operatorname{corad}(G)\) and \(\operatorname{d\acute{e}r}(G)\). The groups \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) and \(\operatorname{corad}(G)\) are tori, which are trivial when \(G\) is split; moreover, there exists an isogeny \(\operatorname{rad}(G) \to \operatorname{corad}(G)\). The \(S\)-group \(\operatorname{d\acute{e}r}(G)\) is semi-simple, and one has \(G/\operatorname{d\acute{e}r}(G) = \operatorname{corad}(G)\); it follows that for every principal homogeneous bundle \(P\) under \(G\), \(P/\operatorname{d\acute{e}r}(G)\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(\operatorname{corad}(G)\). This said, we have:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group of constant type.

(i) The following conditions are equivalent:

(a) \(G\) is locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial.

(b) The torus \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) is so.

(b') The torus \(\operatorname{corad}(G)\) is so.

(c) The Galois covering of \(S\) associated with \(G\) (3.11) is so.

If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), these conditions are also equivalent to

(d) The torus \(T\) is locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial

(ii) Let \(P\) be a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\); in order for \(P\) to be locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial, it is necessary and sufficient that the \(\operatorname{corad}(G)\)-principal bundle \(P/\operatorname{d\acute{e}r}(G)\) be so.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.1.6

The conditions of (i) are satisfied when \(G\) is semi-simple or when \(S\) is locally noetherian and normal (or more generally geometrically unibranch). The conditions of (ii) are satisfied when \(G\) is locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial.

For (i), the first assertion is trivial from (b), the second follows from (c) and Exp. X, 5.14 and 5.15. For (ii), it suffices to remark that, by virtue of theorem 90, a principal bundle under a trivial torus is semi-locally isotrivial.
4.2. Proof: the semi-simple case
Let us first prove, with a view to later reference:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\) (resp. \(B\) a Borel group, resp. \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\)), \(P\) a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\), \(G'\) the twisted form of \(G\) associated with \(P\) (via the morphism \(\operatorname{int} : G \to \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G)\)). One has a canonical isomorphism \[ \begin{gathered} P/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G')\\ (\text{resp. } P/B \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(G'),\\ \text{resp. } P/T \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Kil}}(G')). \end{gathered} \]

By construction, \(G'\) is the quotient of \(P \times_S G\) by a certain action of \(G\) (\((p, g')g = (pg, g^{-1}g'g)\)); one thus has a morphism \(P \times_S G \to G'\), that is to say a morphism \[ P \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_S(G, G'), \] which, as one sees at once, factors through a morphism \[ f : P \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, G'), \] (to verify this assertion, one may assume \(G = P\), in which case one has \(G' = G\), \(f = \operatorname{int}\)). The set-theoretic map \(p \mapsto f(p)(T)\) defines a morphism \[ P \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G'). \] To verify that this morphism induces an isomorphism \(P/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G')\) as announced, one may again assume \(P = G\), in which case one is reduced to Exp. XXII, 5.8.3 (iii). (In fact, loc. cit. ought to be replaced by the statement above). One argues in the same way for \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Kil}}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.2

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a semi-simple \(S\)-group of constant type.

(i) \(G\) is isotrivial.

(ii) Every principal bundle under \(G\) is isotrivial.

Let us prove (i). After possibly making a finite surjective étale extension of the base, we may, by 3.9.2, assume \(G\) quasi-split. But then \(G\) is isotrivial by construction (3.11, the group \(E\) is finite). To prove (ii), we may, by virtue of (i), assume \(G\) split; one is then reduced to:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.2.3

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme. Every principal bundle under a split reductive group is isotrivial.

Indeed, with the notation of 4.2.1, where \(B \supset T\) denotes the canonical Killing couple of the split group \(G\), the \(S\)-prescheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Kil}}(G')\) possesses a section, after a finite surjective étale extension of the base, by virtue of 3.9.2. One may therefore reduce the structural group of \(G\) to \(T\); now \(T\) is trivial, hence \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, T) = 0\) (theorem 90).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme and \[ 1 \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow G' \longrightarrow G'' \longrightarrow 1 \] an exact sequence of \(S\)-preschemes in groups (for (fpqc)), \(G\) being semi-simple of constant type. Let \(P\) be a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G'\); suppose the associated bundle \(P/G\) representable (for example \(G''\) affine over \(S\)). In order for \(P\) to be locally isotrivial (resp. semi-locally isotrivial), it is necessary and sufficient that \(P/G\) be so (as a bundle under \(G'\)).

If \(P\) is trivial, so is \(P/G\), which shows that the condition is necessary. Conversely, suppose \(S\) local (resp. semi-local) and \(P/G\) isotrivial, hence trivialised by a finite surjective étale extension \(S'\) of \(S\). Extending the base to \(S'\), one may reduce the structural group of \(P_{S'}\) to \(G_{S'}\). But \(S'\) is again semi-local and \(G_{S'}\) semi-simple of constant type, hence the bundle obtained is isotrivial (4.2.2).
4.3. Proof: general case. —

Let us first remark that 4.1.5 (ii) follows at once from the application of 4.2.4 to the exact sequence \[ 1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{d\acute{e}r}(G) \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow \operatorname{corad}(G) \longrightarrow 1\,. \] Let us therefore prove (i). If \(G\) is split, \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) and \(\operatorname{corad}(G)\) are trivial, as is \(\operatorname{rev}(G)\); one thus has (a) \(\Rightarrow\) (b), (b'), (c).

One has (c) \(\Rightarrow\) (a). Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be the type of \(G\); one has an exact sequence \[ 1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{ad}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})) \longrightarrow \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow E_S \longrightarrow 1\,. \] Applying 4.2.4 to the bundle \(P = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}), G)\) and to the associated bundle \(\operatorname{rev}(G) = P/\operatorname{ad}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(G))\), one has (c) \(\Rightarrow\) (a).

We have (b) \(\Rightarrow\) (a). It suffices to prove that if \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) is trivial, \(G\) is semi-locally isotrivial. Now let \(G_0 = \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\); consider the category of pairs \((G', f)\), where \(G'\) is a form of \(G_0\) and \(f\) an isomorphism of \(\operatorname{rad}(G_0)\) onto \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\). It is known (2.16) that this category is equivalent to the category of principal homogeneous bundles under a certain \(S\)-group \(H\) which is an extension of a finite twisted constant group by a semi-simple group. It suffices to prove that every principal bundle under \(H\) is semi-locally isotrivial, and this follows at once from 4.2.4.

We have (b') \(\Rightarrow\) (a). One may argue as above (it will moreover be the same group \(H\) that comes in). One may also see that (b) and (b') are equivalent: a torus isogenous to a locally trivial torus is likewise locally trivial (cf. Exp. IX, 2.11 (iii)).
We have (d) \(\Rightarrow\) (a). It suffices to prove that a group of constant type possessing a trivial maximal torus is semi-locally isotrivial; now this follows at once from 2.14.
We have (a) \(\Rightarrow\) (d). It suffices to prove that a maximal torus of a split group is semi-locally isotrivial. Now we have more precisely:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.3.6

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T_0\) a trivial maximal torus of \(G\), \(W_0 = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T_0)/T_0\) (it is a locally constant \(S\)-group, and constant if \(G\) is of constant type, by 2.14), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\).

There exists a morphism \(S' \to S\) which is principal homogeneous under \(W_0\) (hence étale, finite and surjective, and even principal Galois if \(G\) is of constant type), such that \(T_{S'}\) is conjugate to \((T_0)_{S'}\) by an element of \(G(S')\) (and therefore in particular trivial).

Indeed, it is known that \(\underline{\mathrm{Transp}}_G(T_0, T)\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T_0)\) (cf. for example Exp. XI, 5.4 bis). Set \(S' = \underline{\mathrm{Transp}}_G(T_0, T)/T_0\); it is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(W_0\). Extending the base from \(S\) to \(S'\), one may reduce the structure group of \(\underline{\mathrm{Transp}}_G(T_0, T)\) to \(T_0\). But \(S'\) is semi-local and \(T_0\) trivial, hence \(\underline{\mathrm{Transp}}_G(T_0, T)\) possesses a section over \(S'\). Q.E.D.
4.4. Use of the existence of maximal tori
Using Grothendieck's existence theorem for maximal tori (Exp. XIV, 3.20), one can considerably sharpen the preceding results. Let us state straight away:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.4.1

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(\mathscr{R}\) a reduced pinned root datum, \(W\) its Weyl group, \(E\) the group of its automorphisms. (Recall that \(E\) operates naturally on \(W\) and that the semi-direct product \(\mathrm{A} = W \cdot E\) is identified with the group of automorphisms of \(\mathscr{R}\) without its pinning, cf. Exp. XXI, 6.7.2).

(i) Every principal homogeneous bundle under \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\) is trivialised by a principal Galois covering \(S' \to S\) with group \(W\).

(ii) Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathscr{R}\); let \(\operatorname{rev}(G) = \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}), G)\) be the associated Galois covering of \(S\) with group \(E\). Let \(W_0\) be the form of \(W_S\) associated with \(\operatorname{rev}(G)\). There exists a morphism \(S' \to S\), which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(W_0\), such that \(G_{S'}\) is quasi-splittable (i.e. possesses a Borel group).

(iii) Every reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathscr{R}\) is split by a principal Galois covering \(\overline{S} \to S\) with group \(\mathrm{A}\).
Let us first state:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.4.2
