Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(P\) a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\), \(G'\) the twisted form of \(G\) associated with \(P\) (one then has, cf. 4.2.1, a canonical isomorphism \(P/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G')\)). Let \(T'\) be a maximal torus of \(G'\), defining a composite morphism \[ S \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G') \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } P/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T). \] Consider the canonical morphisms \[ P \longrightarrow P/T \longrightarrow P/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T) \] and take their inverse images under the preceding morphism: \[ \xymatrix{ P & P/T & P/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T) \\ H \ar[u] & S' \ar[u] & S. \ar[u] } \] Then \(S'\) (resp. \(H\)) is a principal homogeneous bundle over \(S\) (resp. \(S'\)) under \(W_G(T)\) (resp. \(T_{S'}\)). Moreover, if one lets \(W_G(T)\) operate on \(T\) in the obvious way, the bundle associated with \(S'\) is isomorphic to \(T'\).
The first two assertions are trivial, the last is proved like the corresponding assertion of 2.6.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.4.3

Let \(S\) be a semi-local prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). Suppose that one of the two following conditions is satisfied:

(i) \(T\) is trivial.

(ii) \(T\) is contained in a Borel group of \(G\), and \(G\) is either adjoint or simply connected.

Let moreover \(P\) be a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\). There exists an \(S\)-prescheme \(S'\), which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(W_G(T)\), such that \(P_{S'}\) is trivial.

Indeed, if \(G'\) is the form of \(G\) associated with \(P\), \(G'\) possesses a maximal torus \(T'\) (Exp. XIV, 3.20). Resuming the notation of the preceding proposition, one sees that \(\mathrm{H}^1(S', T_{S'}) = 0\) (by Theorem 90 for (i), by 3.14 for (ii)). The morphism \(H \to S'\) possesses a section, hence \(P_{S'}\) also possesses a section over \(S'\). Q.E.D.

Let us now prove the theorem. Assertion (i) is a special case of the preceding corollary (take \(G = \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\), equipped with its canonical trivial torus). Let us prove (ii). It is known (3.12) that \(G\) is an inner twisted form of \[ G_0 = \mathrm{Q}\text{-}\mathrm{\acute{E}p}_{\operatorname{rev}(G)/S}(\mathscr{R}). \] If \(T_0\) is the canonical maximal torus of \(G_0\), \(W_{G_0}(T_0)\) is indeed the group \(W_0\) described in the statement. The form \(G\) of \(G_0\) corresponds to a principal homogeneous bundle \(P\) under \(\operatorname{ad}(G_0)\) (\(P = \underline{\mathrm{Isomint}}(G_0, G)\)). The group \(W_{\operatorname{ad}(G_0)}(T_0^{\mathrm{ad}})\) is canonically isomorphic to \(W_0\), and one obtains the desired result by applying 4.4.3 to the situation \((\operatorname{ad}(G_0), T_0^{\mathrm{ad}}, P)\), hypothesis (ii) of 4.4.3 being indeed satisfied. Let us finally prove (iii). Let us resume the notation of (ii); we have a diagram \[ \xymatrix{ & \operatorname{rev}(G) \ar[d]^{E_S} & \\ & S & S' \ar[l]^{W_0} } \] It is known that \(G_{S'}\) is isomorphic to \((G_0)_{S'}\) and that \((G_0)_{\operatorname{rev}(G)}\) is splittable. If one sets \(\overline{S} = S' \times_S \operatorname{rev}(G)\), \(G_{\overline{S}}\) is indeed splittable, and it only remains to check that \(\overline{S}\) is indeed a principal Galois covering of \(S\) with group \(\mathrm{A}\), which follows from the following more general lemma (valid of course in any site):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.4.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(H\) two \(S\)-preschemes in groups, \(G \to \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(H)\) an operation of \(G\) on \(H\), \(E\) a principal homogeneous \(G\)-bundle, \(F\) a principal homogeneous \(H_0\)-bundle, where \(H_0\) is the form of \(H\) associated with \(E\). Then \(E \times_S F\) is naturally equipped with a structure of principal homogeneous bundle under the semi-direct product \(H \cdot G\).

Let us write \((e, g) \mapsto eg\) (resp. \((f, u) \mapsto fu\)) for the (right) operation of \(G\) on \(E\) (resp. of \(H_0\) on \(F\)). Let us write \[ p : E \times_S H \longrightarrow H_0 \] for the canonical projection (\(H_0\) is by definition the quotient of \(E \times_S H\) by \(G\) operating on it according to the formula \((e, h)g = (eg, g^{-1}hg)\). Consider the morphism \[ r : \quad E \times_S F \times_S H \times_S G \longrightarrow E \times_S F \] defined set-theoretically by \[ r(e, f, h, g) = (eg, fp(e, h)). \] The morphism \(r\) does define an operation of the semi-direct product \(H \cdot G\) on \(E \times_S F\). Indeed, one has set-theoretically \[ r(r(e, f, h, g), h', g') = (egg', fp(e, h)p(eg, h')); \] But \[ p(e, h)p(eg, h') = p(e, h)p(e, gh'g^{-1}) = p(e, hgh'g^{-1}), \] whence \[ r(r(e, f, h, g), h', g') = r(e, f, hgh'g^{-1}, gg'), \] which is what had to be proved.

To prove now that this law is indeed a law of principal homogeneous bundle, one may suppose that \(E\) and \(F\) are trivial, in which case one sees at once that \(E \times_S F\) is likewise a trivial bundle.

pages.title: 5. Canonical decomposition of an adjoint or simply connected group

blocks.html: 5. Canonical decomposition of an adjoint or simply connected group

In this section, we shall use the results of no 1 to generalise to the case of preschemes a classical decomposition of adjoint (resp. simply connected) groups. In order not to overburden the exposition indefinitely, the proofs are only sketched and the details are left to the reader; in fact it is always a matter of absolutely standard proofs in the theory of principal bundles: reduction of the structure group, twisting, ….

Recall (Exp. XXI, 7.4) that a Dynkin diagram is the disjoint union of its connected components, which are Dynkin diagrams. Moreover, every non-empty connected Dynkin diagram corresponding to a root datum is isomorphic to one of the type diagrams (\(\mathrm{A}_n, \mathrm{B}_n, \ldots, \mathrm{G}_2\)) which were exhibited in Exp. XXI, 7.4.6. In what follows, we shall only be interested in Dynkin diagrams whose connected components are of one of the preceding types. Let \(\mathbf{T}\) be the set of these type diagrams. For every Dynkin diagram \(\mathrm{D}\), let \(n(\mathbf{t})\) be the number of connected components of \(\mathrm{D}\) isomorphic to \(\mathbf{t}\), where \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}\). The type of \(\mathrm{D}\) is by definition \(\sum_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} n(\mathbf{t})\, \mathbf{t}\).

A Dynkin diagram of type \(\mathbf{t}\) is said to be simple of type \(\mathbf{t}\), a Dynkin diagram of type \(n\, \mathbf{t}\) is said to be isotypic of type \(\mathbf{t}\). Let \(\mathrm{D}_0\) be the set of connected components of \(\mathrm{D}\) and let \[ a : \mathrm{D}_0 \longrightarrow \mathbf{T} \] be the obvious map. The type of \(\mathrm{D}\) is nothing but \(\sum_{x \in \mathrm{D}_0} a(x)\).

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(\mathrm{D}\) a \(S\)-Dynkin scheme (satisfying the restrictive condition stated above). The cokernel of the pair of morphisms \(\mathrm{R} \rightrightarrows \mathrm{D}\) (\(\mathrm{R} =\) scheme of the links of \(\mathrm{D}\)) is denoted \(\mathrm{D}_0\). It is the "scheme of connected components" of \(\mathrm{D}\) (it exists trivially when \(\mathrm{D}\) is constant; the general case follows from this by descent); it is a finite twisted constant \(S\)-scheme. We have a canonical morphism \[ a : \mathrm{D}_0 \longrightarrow \mathbf{T}_S. \] For \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}\), set \(a^{-1}(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{D}_{0,\mathbf{t}}\); it is a subscheme of \(\mathrm{D}_0\), whose inverse image in \(\mathrm{D}\), denoted \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathbf{t}}\), is the isotypic component of type \(\mathbf{t}\) of the Dynkin scheme \(\mathrm{D}\). Each \(\mathrm{D}_{\mathbf{t}}\) is a subscheme of \(\mathrm{D}\), and one has \[ \mathrm{D} = \coprod_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \mathrm{D}_{\mathbf{t}}\,. \] Note that the degree of \(\mathrm{D}_{0,\mathbf{t}}\) at \(s \in S\) is \(n(s, \mathbf{t})\), if the type of \(\mathrm{D}\) at \(s\) is \(\sum_{\mathbf{t}} n(s, \mathbf{t})\, \mathbf{t}\).

In what follows, we shall only consider adjoint (resp. simply connected) semi-simple groups. To simplify the language, we shall state the results for adjoint groups; all the statements remain valid if one substitutes throughout simply connected for adjoint.

Recall that a reduced adjoint root datum is determined up to isomorphism by the type of its Dynkin diagrams. One will therefore say that an adjoint root datum \(\mathscr{R}\) (resp. an adjoint semi-simple group \(G\)) is of type \(\sum n(\mathbf{t})\, \mathbf{t}\) if its Dynkin diagrams are (resp. if its type is given by an adjoint root datum of type \(\sum n(\mathbf{t})\, \mathbf{t}\)). One will say that \(\mathscr{R}\) or \(G\) is simple of type \(\mathbf{t}\) (resp. isotypic of type \(\mathbf{t}\)), if its type is \(\mathbf{t}\) (resp. \(n\, \mathbf{t}\), \(n \geqslant 0\)).
If \(G\) is an adjoint semi-simple group, we shall use the symbols \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_{0,\mathbf{t}}(G)\) in the sense defined in 5.2.

Let \(\mathbf{t}_i\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), be distinct elements of \(\mathbf{T}\), and let \(\mathscr{R}_i\) be a pinned adjoint root datum, isotypic of type \(\mathbf{t}_i\). Consider the product \(\mathscr{R} = \mathscr{R}_1 \times \cdots \times \mathscr{R}_n\) (Exp. XXI, 6.4.1). Let \(S\) be a prescheme such that the various \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}_i)\) exist (cf. Exp. XXV). One checks at once that there exists a canonical isomorphism \[ (*) \qquad \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}) = \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}_1) \times_S \cdots \times_S \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}_n). \] Moreover, if \(E_i\) denotes the group of automorphisms of \(\mathscr{R}_i\), \(E\) the group of automorphisms of \(\mathscr{R}\), \(\mathrm{D}_i\) (resp. \(\mathrm{D}\)) the Dynkin diagram of \(\mathscr{R}_i\) (resp. \(\mathscr{R}\)), one has isomorphisms: \[ \begin{gathered} \mathrm{D} = \coprod \mathrm{D}_i, \qquad E = \prod E_i,\\ E \simeq \operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{D}), \qquad E_i \simeq \operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{D}_i). \end{gathered} \] Combining this with \((*)\) and 1.4, one sees that \((*)\) induces an isomorphism \[ \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}) \simeq \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}_1) \times_S \cdots \times_S \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}_n). \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an adjoint semi-simple \(S\)-group. There exists a unique decomposition \[ G \simeq \prod_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} G_{\mathbf{t}}\,, \] where \(G_{\mathbf{t}}\) is an adjoint semi-simple \(S\)-group, isotypic of type \(\mathbf{t}\). Moreover, the preceding decomposition induces isomorphisms \[ \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_{\mathbf{t}}(G) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G_{\mathbf{t}}), \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \simeq \prod_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G_{\mathbf{t}}). \]

This has indeed been proved above when \(G\) is split. In the general case, one may suppose \(G\) of constant type \(\mathscr{R}\). Using the preceding decomposition of \(\underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})\) and 1.17, one deduces the desired decomposition of \(G\). The other results are then proved by descent.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.6

More generally, if \(G\) and \(H\) are two adjoint semi-simple groups, one has canonical isomorphisms as follows (the diagram is commutative): \[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d] & \prod\limits_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G_{\mathbf{t}}, H_{\mathbf{t}}) \ar[d] \\ \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G, H) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_{\wr} & \prod\limits_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \underline{\mathrm{Isomext}}(G_{\mathbf{t}}, H_{\mathbf{t}}) \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G), \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(H)) \ar[r]^-{\sim} & \prod\limits_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G_{\mathbf{t}}), \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(H_{\mathbf{t}})). } \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.7

One can give an intrinsic characterisation of \(G_{\mathbf{t}}\), which we state below without proof: it is the largest reductive subgroup of \(G\) which is invariant (and moreover characteristic) and isotypic of type \(\mathbf{t}\).
The preceding proposition allows one to reduce the study of adjoint semi-simple groups to that of isotypic adjoint semi-simple groups. It is this study that we shall carry out below.

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a reduced pinned adjoint root datum, simple of type \(\mathbf{t}\), \(\mathrm{I}\) a non-empty finite set, \(\mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{I}}\) the root datum product of copies \(\mathscr{R}_i\) of \(\mathscr{R}\), for \(i \in \mathrm{I}\). Let us write \(E\) for the group of automorphisms of \(\mathscr{R}\), which is identified with the group of automorphisms of the Dynkin diagram \(\mathrm{D}\) of \(\mathscr{R}\). The Dynkin diagram of \(\mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{I}}\) is identified with \(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{I}}\), which shows that one has an exact sequence: \[ 1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{D})^{\mathrm{I}} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{I}}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{I}) \longrightarrow 1\,, \] where \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{I})\) denotes the group of permutations of \(\mathrm{I}\). It follows that the canonical isomorphism \[ \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})^{\mathrm{I}} \simeq \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{I}}) \] induces an exact sequence \[ 1 \longrightarrow \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R})^{\mathrm{I}} \longrightarrow \underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{I}}) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathrm{I}_S) \longrightarrow 1\,, \] the last group being the constant \(S\)-group associated with \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathrm{I})\). Note on the other hand that \(\mathrm{I}\) is canonically identified with the set of connected components of \(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{I}}\). If \(G\) is a semi-simple \(S\)-group of type \(\mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{I}}\), defining (cf. 1.17) a principal homogeneous bundle \(P\) under \(\underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{I}})\), the definition of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) by descent (3.7), and that of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\) (5.2), show that the bundle associated with \(P\) by the morphism \(\underline{\underline{\mathrm{A}}}_S(\mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{I}}) \to \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathrm{I}_S)\) is nothing but \(\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_S(\mathrm{I}_S, \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G))\), corresponding to the form \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\) of \(\mathrm{I}_S\). Using once again the equivalence of categories 1.17 and the preceding exact sequence, one deduces by a formal argument that there exists a reductive \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\)-group of type \(\mathscr{R}\), say \(G_0\), and an \(S\)-isomorphism \(G \simeq \prod_{\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)/S} G_0\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an adjoint semi-simple \(S\)-group, isotypic of type \(\mathbf{t}\). There exist an adjoint semi-simple \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\)-group \(G_0\), simple of type \(\mathbf{t}\), and an \(S\)-isomorphism (both unique) \[ G \simeq \prod_{\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)/S} G_0. \] Moreover, this isomorphism induces an exact sequence \[ 1 \longrightarrow \prod_{\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)/S} \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G_0) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)) \longrightarrow 1\,. \]

One may obviously suppose \(G\) of constant type \(n\, \mathbf{t}\). The first assertion has already been proved (the uniqueness assertion is obvious). The second then follows from the split case by descent.
One may combine 5.5 and 5.9:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.10

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) an adjoint semi-simple \(S\)-group, \(\mathfrak{D} = \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) its Dynkin scheme.

(i) There exists a canonical decomposition \[ G \simeq \prod_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \prod_{\mathfrak{D}_{0,\mathbf{t}}/S} G_{0,\mathbf{t}} \simeq \prod_{\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)/S} G_0\,, \] where each \(G_{0,\mathbf{t}}\) is a simple adjoint \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_{0,\mathbf{t}}(G)\)-group of type \(\mathbf{t}\) (resp. where \(G_0\) is an adjoint semi-simple \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\)-group whose type at \(x \in \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\) is \(a(x) \in \mathbf{T}\) (the morphism \(a : \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G) \to \mathbf{T}_S\) was defined in 5.2)).

(ii) The preceding decompositions induce isomorphic exact sequences (written vertically): \[ \xymatrix{ 1 \ar[d] & 1 \ar[d] \\ \prod\limits_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \prod\limits_{\mathfrak{D}_{0,\mathbf{t}}/S} \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{gr.}}(G_{0,\mathbf{t}}) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d] & \prod\limits_{\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)/S} \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathrm{gr.}}(G_0) \ar[d] \\ \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G) \ar[d] \\ \prod\limits_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_S(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_{0,\mathbf{t}}(G)) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d] & \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S,a}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)) \ar[d] \\ 1 & 1 } \] where \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S,a}(\mathrm{D}_0)\) denotes the scheme of automorphisms of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\) which commute with the morphism \(a : \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G) \to \mathbf{T}_S\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.11

Under the preceding conditions, the three following categories are equivalent:

(i) the category of principal homogeneous bundles under \(G\).

(ii) the category of principal homogeneous bundles under \(G_0\).

(iii) the product category, for \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}\), of the categories of principal homogeneous bundles under the \(G_{0,\mathbf{t}}\).
This follows formally from the preceding decompositions and from 8.4.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.12

One has canonical isomorphisms \[ \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G) \simeq \prod_{\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}} \prod_{\mathfrak{D}_{0,\mathbf{t}}/S} \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G_{0,\mathbf{t}}) \simeq \prod_{\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)/S} \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G_0), \] and likewise on replacing \(\underline{\mathrm{Tor}}\) by \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}\) (resp. \(\underline{\mathrm{Kil}}\)).
Trivial from the split case.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.13

The canonical morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G) \] allows one to regard \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) as a \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}_0(G)\)-Dynkin scheme; in fact it is the Dynkin scheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G_0)\) of \(G_0\).

Likewise, if \(T \subset B\) is a Killing couple of \(G\), corresponding canonically to the Killing couple \(T_0 \subset B_0\) of \(G_0\), one checks that the obstructions to the quasi-splitting of \(G\) and \(G_0\), which lie (3.9) in \(\operatorname{Pic}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) = \operatorname{Pic}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G_0))\), coincide. One deduces from this:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.14

The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(G\) is quasi-splittable,

(ii) \(G_0\) is quasi-splittable,

(iii) each \(G_{0,\mathbf{t}}\), \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbf{T}\), is quasi-splittable.

pages.title: 6. Automorphisms of the Borel groups of reductive groups

blocks.html: 6. Automorphisms of the Borel groups of reductive groups

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group, \(R_0\) a system of simple roots of \(R\), \(B\) the corresponding Borel group. Then \(B^u\) is generated as a (fppf) sheaf in groups by the \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\).

Let \(H\) be the subsheaf in groups of \(B^u\) generated by the \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\). Let us prove \(H \supset U_\beta\) by induction on the integer \(> 0\), \(\operatorname{ord}_{R_0}(\beta)\) (cf. Exp. XXI, 3.2.15). The assertion holds by hypothesis for \(\operatorname{ord}(\beta) = 1\). Suppose then \(\operatorname{ord}(\beta) > 1\) and \(U_\gamma \subset H\) whenever \(\operatorname{ord}(\gamma) < \operatorname{ord}(\beta)\). There exists \(\alpha \in R_0\) such that \(\beta - \alpha \in R_+\) (Exp. XXI, 3.1.1). Let \(p\) be the largest integer such that \(\beta - p\,\alpha = \beta' \in R_+\). One has \(U_\alpha, U_{\beta'} \subset H\), \(\beta' - \alpha \notin R\). We are thus reduced to proving:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.2

Let us resume the notation of Exp. XXIII, 6.4. Suppose \(p = 1\), that is to say \(\beta - \alpha\) not a root. If \(H\) is a subsheaf in groups of \(B^u\) such that \(U_\alpha, U_\beta \subset H\), then \(U_{i\alpha + j\beta} \subset H\) whenever \(i\alpha + j\beta \in R\), \(i > 0\), \(j > 0\).
Let us distinguish four cases according to the value of \(q = 0, 1, 2, 3\). In what follows \(x\) and \(y\) denote two arbitrary sections of \(\mathbf{G}_{a,S'}\), \(S' \to S\).
If \(q = 0\), there is nothing to prove.
If \(q = 1\), one has \(p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm x) = p_\beta(-1)\,p_\alpha(-x)\,p_\beta(1)\,p_\alpha(x) \in H(S')\), hence \(U_{\alpha+\beta} \subset H\).

If \(q = 2\), one has likewise \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(\pm x^2 y) = p_\beta(-y)\, p_\alpha(-x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) \in H(S'), \] whence, after possibly changing certain signs \[ F(x, y) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 y) \in H(S'). \] Now one has at once \(F(x, 1)F(-1, x) = p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 - x)\). If \(a \in \mathbf{G}_a(S)\), the equation \(X^2 - X = a\) defines a free and surjective extension of \(S\) (it is \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathscr{O}_S[X]/(X^2 - X - a)\)); one therefore has \(p_{2\alpha+\beta}(a) \in H(S')\), hence \(U_{2\alpha+\beta} \subset H\), and hence also \(U_{\alpha+\beta} \subset H\) (since \(F(1, a) \in H(S')\)).

If \(q = 3\), one has likewise \[ F(x, y) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x^3 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(x^3 y^2) \in H(S'); \] but \[ p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(\pm x) = F(1, 1)^{-1}\, p_\beta(-x)\, F(1, 1)\, p_\beta(x) \in H(S'), \] hence also \[ K(x, y) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x^3 y) \in H(S'). \] We have thus already proved \(U_{3\alpha+2\beta} \subset H\). Computing then \[ K(x + y, 1)\, K(-x, 1)\, K(1, y)^{-1} \] modulo \(U_{3\alpha+2\beta}\), one finds \[ p_{2\alpha+\beta}(2x^2 + y^2 + 2xy - y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(y^3 + 3xy^2 + 3x^2 y - y) \in H(S'). \] If \(a \in \mathbf{G}_a(S)\), the "equations" \[ \begin{aligned} x^2 &= -xy - y + 1 - a\\ y^2 &= 3y - 2 + 3a \end{aligned} \] define a free and surjective extension of \(S\); the preceding expression then gives \(p_{3\alpha+\beta}(a) \in H(S')\). We have thus proved \[ U_{3\alpha+\beta},\quad U_{3\alpha+2\beta} \subset H, \qquad p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(xy^2) \in H(S'), \] and we are reduced to the preceding computation.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.2.1

The preceding proof shows that one could have replaced the hypothesis "\(H \supset U_\alpha, U_\beta\)" by "\(H \supset U_\alpha\) or \(U_\beta\), and \(H\) is invariant under \(\operatorname{int}(U_\alpha)\) and \(\operatorname{int}(U_\beta)\)".

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 6.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two semi-simple \(S\)-groups, \(B\) (resp. \(B'\)) a Borel subgroup of \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)). Every isomorphism \(B \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } B'\) is induced by a unique isomorphism \(G \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } G'\).

The assertion is local for the étale topology and one may suppose \(G\) split: \(G = (G, T, M, R)\), \(B\) being defined by the system of positive roots \(R_+\) of \(R\). The given isomorphism \(u : B \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } B'\) induces an isomorphism of \(T\) onto a maximal torus \(T'\) of \(B'\), hence of \(G'\). The given isomorphism \(T \simeq \mathrm{D}_S(M)\) yields an isomorphism \(T' \simeq \mathrm{D}_S(M)\) in which the elements of \(R_+\) become the constant roots of \(B'\) relative to \(T'\), hence the elements of \(R\) the constant roots of \(G'\) relative to \(T'\). Since \(G\) and \(G'\) are semi-simple, the coroots are determined by duality (Exp. XXI, 1.2.5), which proves that \((T', M, R)\) is a splitting of \(G'\) such that \(\mathscr{R}(G) = \mathscr{R}(G')\).

Applying Exp. XXIII, 5.1 (Uniqueness theorem), one deduces that there exists a unique isomorphism \(G \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } G'\) coinciding with \(u\) on \(T\) and the \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\). By 5.1, the restriction of this isomorphism to \(B\) is \(u\). Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.3.1

(i) Using Exp. XXII, 4.1.9 and arguing as in loc. cit. 4.2.12, one may in the statement of the theorem replace "isomorphism" by "isogeny" (resp. "central isogeny").

(ii) The theorem is false for reductive groups. Take for example \(G = G' = \mathrm{SL}_2 \times \mathbf{G}_m\) identified with the group of matrices \[ \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & b & 0\\ c & d & 0\\ 0 & 0 & h \end{pmatrix} \;\middle|\; ad - bc = 1,\ h \text{ invertible} \right\}; \] take for \(B = B'\) the Borel group defined by \(c = 0\) and for \(u\) the automorphism of \(B\): \(u(a, b, d, h) = (a, b, d, ah)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.4

The functor \((G, B) \mapsto B\) from the category of pairs: (semi-simple \(S\)-groups, Borel group) to the category of \(S\)-preschemes in groups (the morphisms being the isomorphisms) is fully faithful.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a semi-simple \(S\)-group, \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\), \(B'\) an \(S\)-group locally isomorphic to \(B\) for (fpqc). Then \(B'\) is locally isomorphic to \(B\) for the local finite étale topology and there exists a semi-simple \(S\)-group \(G'\) of which \(B'\) is a Borel group; \(G'\) is unique up to a unique isomorphism inducing the identity on \(B'\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a semi-simple \(S\)-group, \(B\) a Borel group of \(G\). Then \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(B)\) is representable by an affine and smooth \(S\)-prescheme, \(\underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(B)\) is representable by an étale and finite \(S\)-prescheme, and the obvious morphisms induce an isomorphism of exact sequences \[ \xymatrix{ 1 \ar[r] & B^{\mathrm{ad}} \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\wr} & \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, B) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\wr} & \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(G) \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\wr} & 1 \\ 1 \ar[r] & B^{\mathrm{ad}} \ar[r] & \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(B) \ar[r] & \underline{\mathrm{Autext}}(B) \ar[r] & 1. } \]
This follows at once from 2.1 and the preceding results. We leave to the reader the task of developing the analogues of the results of Nos 1, 2, 3, 4 in the framework above.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.7

If \(S\) is a prescheme and \(B\) an \(S\)-group, \(B\) can therefore be the Borel group of only one semi-simple group, entirely determined by \(B\). It thus remains to characterise those \(S\)-groups \(B\) which really are Borel groups of semi-simple groups. The question does not seem to admit a simple answer. Let us point out for instance that there exist smooth affine \(S\)-groups, extensions of a trivial torus and additive groups (even defining a half-system of roots), all of whose fibres are Borel groups of semi-simple groups, but which are not the Borel group of a semi-simple group. For example, take the canonical Borel group of a group of type \(\mathrm{B}_2\) split over the scheme of dual numbers over a field \(k\), and modify the constant 2 in the second commutation relation of Exp. XXIII, 3.3.1 (iii) by replacing it by a different scalar, equal to 2 on the special fibre. The special fibre of the group so obtained will indeed be a Borel group of a semi-simple group, but the group itself will not be one. The cohomological translation of this fact (cf. Exp. III, 3.10) is the following:

let \(k\) be a field, \(G\) a semi-simple \(k\)-group of type \(\mathrm{B}_2\), \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\); then \(\mathrm{H}^2(B, \operatorname{Lie}(B/k)) \ne 0\).

pages.title: 7. Representability of the functors \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\), for \(G\) reductive

blocks.html: 7. Representability of the functors \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\), for \(G\) reductive
7.1. The split case

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group, \(T\) its maximal torus, \(R_0\) the set of simple roots and, for \(\alpha \in R_0\), \[ u_\alpha \in U_\alpha^*(S), \qquad w_\alpha \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T)(S), \] the elements defined by the pinning.

Let on the other hand \(H\) be an \(S\)-group prescheme; we are interested in the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\), and more precisely in the morphism \[ q : \quad \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, H). \] So let \[ f_T : T \longrightarrow H \] be an \(S\)-homomorphism, and consider \(q^{-1}(f_T) = \mathscr{F}\). It is the functor defined by \[ \mathscr{F}(S') = \{ f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S'\text{-gr.}}(G_{S'}, H_{S'}) \mid f = (f_T)_{S'} \text{ on } T_{S'} \}. \] We have a morphism of \(S\)-functors \[ i : \mathscr{F} \longrightarrow H^{2n}\,, \] where \(n = \operatorname{Card}(R_0)\), defined set-theoretically by \(i(f) = (f(u_\alpha), f(w_\alpha))\). By virtue of Exp. XXIII, 1.9, \(i\) is moreover a monomorphism.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.1.2

If \(H\) is separated over \(S\), then \(\mathscr{F}\) is representable and \(i\) is a closed immersion.

The usual technique of relative representability shows us that it suffices to prove that, given sections \[ v_\alpha, h_\alpha \in H(S), \qquad \text{for}\quad \alpha \in R_0, \] the \(S\)-preschemes \(S'\) such that there exists an \(S'\)-homomorphism \[ f : G_{S'} \longrightarrow H_{S'} \] extending \((f_T)_{S'}\) and satisfying \(f(u_\alpha) = v_\alpha\), \(f(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha\), are exactly those which factor through a certain closed sub-prescheme of \(S\). We may obviously assume \(S\) affine.

To simplify what follows, let us say that a morphism \(X \to Y\) of affine schemes satisfies condition (L) if \(Y\) is the spectrum of an \(\mathscr{O}(X)\)-algebra which is a free \(\mathscr{O}(X)\)-module. It is clear that if one restricts oneself to the category of affine schemes, a product, or a composite, of morphisms satisfying (L) satisfies (L), and that (L) is stable under base extension.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.1.3

Assume \(S\) affine, and let \(\alpha \in R_0\). Consider the morphism \[ a : T \times_S T \longrightarrow \mathbf{G}_{a,S} \] defined set-theoretically by \(a(t, t') = \alpha(t) + \alpha(t')\).

(i) \(a\) is faithfully flat and of finite presentation.

(ii) Let \(R\) be the fibre square of \(a\). The structural morphism \(R \to S\) satisfies (L).

It is first of all clear that the morphism \(a\) is surjective, since \(\alpha : T \to \mathbf{G}_{m,S}\) is. It is trivial that \(a\) is of finite presentation. Since \(\alpha\) satisfies (L), it suffices, in order to prove (i) and (ii), to show that the morphism \[ u : \mathbf{G}_{m,S}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbf{G}_{a,S} \] defined set-theoretically by \(u(x, y) = x + y\) satisfies (L). In other words, it suffices to check that for every ring \(\mathrm{A}\), the ring \(\mathrm{A}[X, Y, X^{-1}, Y^{-1}]\) is a free module over its subring \(\mathrm{A}[X + Y]\). Now the elements \((XY)^p\), \((XY)^p X\), \(p \in \mathbf{Z}\) form a basis. Indeed, it suffices to check that for every \(q \in \mathbf{Z}\), and every family \(\{a_{ij} \in \mathrm{A} \mid i, j \in \mathbf{Z}\}\), there exist elements \(b_{n,p}, c_{n,p} \in \mathrm{A}\), \(0 \leqslant n \leqslant q\), \(p \in \mathbf{Z}\), unique, such that \[ \sum_{-q \leqslant i - j \leqslant q + 1} a_{ij} X^i Y^j = \sum_{\substack{0 \leqslant n \leqslant q\\ p \in \mathbf{Z}}} \Bigl( b_{n,p} (X + Y)^n (XY)^p X + c_{n,p} (X + Y)^n (XY)^p \Bigr). \] Let us prove this assertion by ascending induction on \(q\). It is trivial for \(q \leqslant -1\); assume \(q \geqslant 0\) (and hence \(q + 1 > -q\)) and assume the assertion true for \(q - 1\). Taking on both sides the terms of the form \(X^a Y^b\) with \(a - b = q + 1\), then with \(a - b = -q\), one immediately obtains \[ a_{q+i+1,i} = b_{q,i} \qquad \text{and} \qquad q_{i,i+p} = c_{q,i}\,. \] This shows first of all that if there is a solution, then the \(b_{q,i}\) and \(c_{q,i}\) are determined by the preceding relations. Subtracting then from both sides \[ b_{q,i}(X + Y)^q (XY)^i X + c_{q,i}(X + Y)^q (XY)^i, \] one is reduced to the assertions of existence and uniqueness already proved by the induction hypothesis.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.1.4

Let \(\alpha \in R_0\), and let \(b : T \times_S T \to H\) be the morphism defined set-theoretically by \[ b(t, t') = \bigl(\operatorname{int}(f_T(t)) v_\alpha\bigr) \bigl(\operatorname{int}(f_T(t')) v_\alpha\bigr). \] Let \(f_\alpha : U_\alpha \to H\) be an \(S\)-morphism. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(f_\alpha\) is a group morphism; one has \(f_\alpha(u_\alpha) = v_\alpha\); one has \[ f_T(t) f_\alpha(x) f_T(t)^{-1} = f_\alpha(\alpha(t) x) \] for all \(t \in T(S')\), \(x \in U_\alpha(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

(ii) One has \(f_\alpha(u_\alpha) = v_\alpha\) and the relation \[ f_\alpha\bigl(a(t, t') u_\alpha\bigr) = b(t, t') \] for all \(t, t' \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

If \(f_\alpha\) satisfies (i), one has \(f_\alpha(\alpha(t) u_\alpha) = \operatorname{int}(f_T(t)) v_\alpha\), which entails (ii) at once. Conversely, assume (ii) satisfied and let us prove the various conditions of (i); let us first prove the last one. Since \(a\) is covering for (fpqc), it suffices to prove that if \(t, t', t'' \in T(S')\), one has \[ f_T(t)\, f_\alpha\bigl(a(t', t'') u_\alpha\bigr)\, f_T(t)^{-1} = f_\alpha\bigl(\alpha(t)\, a(t', t'')\, u_\alpha\bigr); \] now this can also be written \[ f_T(t)\, b(t', t'')\, f_T(t)^{-1} = b(tt', tt''), \] a property evident from the definition of \(b\). It remains to prove that \(f_\alpha\) is a group morphism. Now the preceding property gives at once \[ f_\alpha\bigl(\alpha(t) u_\alpha\bigr) f_\alpha\bigl(\alpha(t') u_\alpha\bigr) = \bigl(\operatorname{int}(f_T(t)) f_\alpha(u_\alpha)\bigr) \cdot \bigl(\operatorname{int}(f_T(t')) f_\alpha(u_\alpha)\bigr) = b(t, t') = f_\alpha\bigl(\alpha(t) u_\alpha + \alpha(t)\alpha(t) v_\alpha\bigr). \] One therefore has \(f_\alpha(x + x') = f_\alpha(x) f_\alpha(x')\), whenever \(x\) and \(x'\) are sections of the open set \(U_\alpha^*\) of \(U_\alpha\), which is schematically dense; one then concludes by Exp. XVIII, 1.4.

Let us fix provisionally an \(\alpha \in R_0\). The morphism \(a\) is faithfully flat and quasi-compact, so \(\mathbf{G}_{a,S}\) is identified with the quotient of \(T \times_S T\) by the equivalence relation \(R\) defined by \(a\). Let \[ R \mathrel{\underset{i_2}{\overset{i_1}{\rightrightarrows}}} T \times_S T \] be this equivalence relation.

For the morphism \(b\) to factor through \(a\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(b \circ i_1 = b \circ i_2\); in other words, if one denotes by \(K\) the kernel of the pair of morphisms \[ R \mathrel{\underset{b \circ i_2}{\overset{b \circ i_1}{\rightrightarrows}}} H\,, \] it is necessary and sufficient that \(K = R\). Now \(H\) is assumed separated over \(S\), so \(K\) is a closed sub-prescheme of \(R\). On the other hand, \(R\) is essentially free over \(S\) (7.1.3).

If \(S'\) is an \(S\)-prescheme, in order for there to exist over \(S'\) an \(f_\alpha\) satisfying the conditions of 7.1.4 (i) (and then necessarily unique), it is necessary and sufficient that \(K_{S'} = R_{S'}\), and that the morphism \(f_\alpha\) obtained satisfy \(f_\alpha(u_\alpha) = v_\alpha\).

The first condition is equivalent to the fact that \(S' \to S\) factors through a certain closed sub-prescheme of \(S\) (Exp. VIII, 6.4); if one replaces \(S\) by this closed sub-prescheme, the second condition again defines a closed sub-prescheme of \(S\) (equality of two sections of \(H\), and \(H\) is assumed separated over \(S\)).

After possibly replacing \(S\) by this closed sub-prescheme, we may therefore assume that there exists a morphism \(f_\alpha : U_\alpha \to H\) satisfying the conditions of 7.1.4 (i). Taking the intersection of the sub-preschemes of \(S\) obtained for each \(\alpha \in R_0\), we may assume this condition satisfied for every \(\alpha \in R_0\).

Likewise, consider for each \(\alpha \in R_0\) the two morphisms of \(S\)-groups \[ f_T \circ \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha),\ \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha) \circ f_T : \quad T \longrightarrow H. \] Since \(H\) is separated over \(S\) and \(T\) essentially free over \(S\), the same argument as above shows that, after possibly replacing \(S\) by a closed sub-prescheme, we may assume that for every \(\alpha \in R_0\) one has \[ f_T \circ \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) = \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha) \circ f_T. \]

Using now the theorem on generators and relations (Exp. XXIII, 3.5), one sees that there exists a group homomorphism \(f : G \to H\) satisfying the required conditions if and only if a certain finite set of algebraic relations \[ \mathrm{R}_i\bigl((h_\alpha), (v_\alpha), (f_T(\alpha^*(-1)))\bigr) = e \] (between the sections \(h_\alpha\), \(v_\alpha\), \(f_T(\alpha^*(-1))\) (\(\alpha \in R_0\),) of \(H\)) is satisfied. Since \(H\) is separated over \(S\), this again defines a closed sub-prescheme of \(S\), and we are done.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.1.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a split reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) its maximal torus, \(H\) an \(S\)-group prescheme separated over \(S\). Let on the other hand \(\mathscr{P}\) be a property of morphisms such that:

(i) A closed immersion satisfies \(\mathscr{P}\).

(ii) The composite of two morphisms satisfying \(\mathscr{P}\) also satisfies \(\mathscr{P}\).

(iii) \(\mathscr{P}\) is stable under base change.

(iv) The structural morphism \(H \to S\) satisfies \(\mathscr{P}\).

Then the canonical morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, H) \] is representable by separated morphisms satisfying \(\mathscr{P}\).
Indeed, we may assume \(G\) pinned; the structural morphism \(H^{2n} \to S\) satisfies \(\mathscr{P}\) and one concludes by 7.1.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.1.10

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a split reductive \(S\)-group, and \(H\) an \(S\)-group prescheme smooth and quasi-separated over \(S\) with affine fibres. Then the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme locally of finite presentation and separated over \(S\).

Indeed, since \(H\) is smooth and quasi-separated over \(S\), one may consider its identity component \(H^0\), which is separated, of finite presentation and with affine fibres (Exp. VI). Since \(G\) has connected fibres, one may replace \(H\) by \(H^0\). Since \(G\) and \(H\) are then of finite presentation, one may assume \(S\) noetherian, and one applies 7.1.9 taking for \(\mathscr{P}\) the property "of finite type". But, by Exp. XV, 8.9, one knows that \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme separated and locally of finite type.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.1.11

If \(H\) is affine over \(S\), one may replace the reference to Exp. XV by Exp. IX, 4.2.
7.2. General case

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). Let on the other hand \(H\) be an \(S\)-group prescheme such that the structural morphism \(H \to S\) satisfies the following condition:

(+) Each point \(s \in S\) has an open neighbourhood \(U\) such that the morphism \(H_U \to U\) is quasi-projective.

Then the canonical morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, H) \] is representable by morphisms satisfying (+).

When \(G\) is splittable relative to \(T\), one applies 7.1.9 taking for \(\mathscr{P}\) property (+) above. When \(G\) is locally isotrivial, for example semi-simple (4.2.2), one remarks that the assertion of the theorem is local for the local finite étale topology (indeed, the property of being quasi-projective is local for the global finite étale topology and ensures the effectiveness of descent for this topology, cf. SGA 1, VIII, 7.7). Finally, in the general case, one uses the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.2.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(G'\) the derived group of \(G\) (Exp. XXII, 6.2), \(T' = T \cap G\) the maximal torus of \(G'\) corresponding to \(T\) (Exp. XXII, 6.2.8). Then the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ G & G' \ar[l] \\ T \ar[u] & T' \ar[l] \ar[u] } \] is an amalgamated sum in the category of \(S\)-group sheaves: that is to say, for every \(S\)-group sheaf \(H\), the following square is cartesian: \[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \operatorname{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G', H) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T, H) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(T', H). } \]

Indeed, if \(\operatorname{rad}(G)\) is the radical of \(G\), then \(\operatorname{rad}(G) \subset T\), so \[ \operatorname{rad}(G) \cap G' = \operatorname{rad}(G) \cap T' = K, \] and the product in \(G\) induces isogenies (Exp. XXII, 6.2) \[ i : G' \times_S \operatorname{rad}(G) \longrightarrow G, \qquad j : T' \times_S \operatorname{rad}(G) \longrightarrow T\,. \] Let \(f_{G'} : G' \to H\), \(f_T : T \to H\), and \(f_{T'} : T' \to H\) be homomorphisms such that \(f_{G'}|_{T'} = f_T|_{T'} = f_{T'}\). Let us show that there exists a unique homomorphism \(f : G \to H\) inducing \(f_{G'}\) and \(f_T\). Let \(f_{\mathrm{rad}} = f_T|_{\operatorname{rad}(G)}\) and let \[ f_1 = f_{G'} \cdot f_{\mathrm{rad}} : \quad G' \times_S \operatorname{rad}(G) \longrightarrow H. \] For \(f\) to exist (and it will obviously be unique), it is necessary and sufficient that \(f_1\) induce the identity on the kernel of \(i\), that is to say that \(f_{G'}\) and \(f_{\mathrm{rad}}\) coincide on \(K\); but the existence of \(f_T\) shows by the same argument that \(f_{T'}\) and \(f_{\mathrm{rad}}\) coincide on \(K\). It only remains to remark that \(f_{G'}\) and \(f_{T'}\) obviously coincide on \(K \subset T'\).
Arguing now as in 7.1.10, one deduces from 7.2.1:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.2.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(H\) an \(S\)-group prescheme, smooth and quasi-projective over \(S\) with affine fibres. Then \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme locally of finite presentation and separated over \(S\).
7.3. Phenomena special to characteristic 0

If \(G\) and \(H\) are two smooth \(S\)-groups, \(\mathfrak{g}\) and \(\mathfrak{h}\) their Lie Algebras, one has a canonical morphism \[ \operatorname{Lie} : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{O}_S\text{-Alg. de Lie}}(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}), \] where the right-hand side has an obvious definition.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.3.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme of characteristic 0 (i.e. a \(\mathbf{Q}\)-prescheme), \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(H\) an \(S\)-group prescheme smooth and quasi-projective over \(S\) with affine fibres.

(i) \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme smooth and separated over \(S\).

(ii) If \(G\) is semi-simple, this prescheme is affine and of finite presentation over \(S\).

(iii) If \(G\) is simply connected (Exp. XXII, 4.3.3), the canonical morphism \[ \operatorname{Lie} : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{O}_S\text{-Alg. de Lie}}(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}) \] is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.3.2

Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic 0, \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group, \(V\) a finite-dimensional \(k\)-vector space, \(G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)\) a linear representation of \(G\) in \(V\). One has \[ \mathrm{H}^0(G, V) = \mathrm{H}^0(\mathfrak{g}, V), \qquad \mathrm{H}^i(G, V) = 0, \quad \text{for } i > 0. \]

The first relation is true in general for a smooth connected group (Exp. VI); in the case of a reductive group, one may prove it as follows: one may assume \(k\) algebraically closed, hence \(G\) splittable, hence \(G\) generated by subgroups isomorphic to \(\mathbf{G}_{m,k}\), and it suffices to check the assertion for this group, which is easy. From this first relation it follows that \(\mathrm{H}^0(G, V)\) is an exact functor in \(V\) when \(G\) is semi-simple; \(\mathfrak{g}\) is indeed then a semi-simple Lie Algebra and one applies Bourbaki, Lie, Chapter I, § 6, Exercise 1, (b). The assertion remains true when \(G\) is reductive; indeed, if one introduces the radical \(R\) of \(G\) and the quotient \(G/R\), which is semi-simple, one has \(\mathrm{H}^0(G, V) = \mathrm{H}^0(G/R, \mathrm{H}^0(R, V))\), and \(\mathrm{H}^0(G, -)\) is a composite of two exact functors. Applying then Exp. I, 5.3.1, one deduces \(\mathrm{H}^i(G, V) = 0\) for \(i > 0\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.3.3

Under the preceding conditions, if \(G\) is semi-simple, one has \(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathfrak{g}, V) = \mathrm{H}^2(\mathfrak{g}, V) = 0\), cf. [BLie], loc. cit. (b) and (d).

Let us now prove the proposition. We already know, by 7.2.3, that \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme locally of finite presentation and separated over \(S\); to show that it is smooth, it suffices to prove that it is infinitesimally smooth (Exp. XI, 1.8), which follows from Exp. III, 2.8 (i) by 7.3.2. We have thus proved (i).

Let us show that (ii) follows from (iii). It suffices first to prove that \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) is affine over \(S\); it will then be of finite presentation over \(S\), since it is smooth over \(S\) by (i); in any case \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{O}_S\text{-Alg. de Lie}}(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h})\) is representable by a closed sub-prescheme of \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{O}_S\text{-Mod.}}(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}) \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathfrak{g}^\vee \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_S} \mathfrak{h}) \] which is an affine \(S\)-prescheme, and the desired conclusion appears when \(G\) is simply connected.

In the general case, one may assume \(G\) split, so that \(G \simeq \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathscr{R})\); introducing the simply connected root datum \(\operatorname{scon}(\mathscr{R})\) (Exp. XXI, 6.5.5), and using the existence theorem (Exp. XXV, 1.1), one constructs a simply connected \(S\)-group \(\overline{G}\) and a central isogeny \(\overline{G} \to G\). The kernel \(K\) of this isogeny is a finite diagonalizable \(S\)-group (hence a twisted constant \(S\)-group, \(S\) being of characteristic 0) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(K, H)\) is (trivially) representable by a separated \(S\)-prescheme (if \(K \simeq (\mathbf{Z}/n\mathbf{Z})_S\), then \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(K, H)\) is isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Ker}(H \xrightarrow{\ n\ } H)\)). One has an exact sequence of "pointed \(S\)-preschemes": \[ 1 \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \xrightarrow{\ u\ } \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\overline{G}, H) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(K, H), \] hence \(u\) is a closed immersion, hence \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) is affine over \(S\).

Let us finally prove (iii). Arguing as in the proof of (i) and using 7.3.3, one can show that the \(S\)-prescheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{O}_S\text{-Alg. de Lie}}(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h})\) is smooth over \(S\). To prove (iii), one may therefore assume that \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), where \(k\) is an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0; it even suffices to prove that \(\operatorname{Lie}\) is bijective on the points with values in \(k\) and that it induces a bijection on the tangent spaces at two corresponding points. Let us first show that \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-gr.}}(G, H) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-Alg. de Lie}}(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}) \] is bijective.

If \(u\) is a homomorphism from \(G\) into \(H\), the graph of \(u\) is a connected subgroup of \(G \times_k H\) which is determined by its Lie algebra, which is the graph of \(\operatorname{Lie}(u)\); the map is therefore injective. Conversely, if \(v : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{h}\) is a homomorphism of Lie Algebras, the graph \(\mathfrak{k}\) of \(v\) is a Lie subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{g} \times \mathfrak{h}\); since \(\mathfrak{g}\) is its own derived algebra, \(\mathfrak{k}\) is its own derived algebra, hence (CHEVALLEY, Théorie des groupes de Lie, Tome 2, § 14, Th. 15) is algebraic. It is therefore the Lie algebra of a connected subgroup \(K\) of \(G \times_k H\). Since \[ \dim(K) = \dim(\mathfrak{k}) = \dim(\mathfrak{g}) = \dim(G) \] and since \(K \cap H\) is finite (for its Lie algebra is zero), the canonical morphism \(\mathrm{pr}_1 : K \to G\) is finite and dominant; since \(G\) is connected, it is surjective; it is therefore an isogeny. Since \(G\) is simply connected, it is an isomorphism (cf. Exp. XXI, 6.2.7) and \(K\) is the graph of a homomorphism of \(k\)-groups \(u : G \to H\) such that \(\operatorname{Lie}(u) = v\).

Finally, let \(u : G \to H\) be a homomorphism. The tangent space to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) at \(u\) is identified with \(\mathrm{Z}^1(G, \mathfrak{h})\) (cf. Exp. II, 4.2; \(G\) operates on \(\mathfrak{h}\) by \(\operatorname{Ad}_H \circ u\)); in the same way, one can prove that the tangent space to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-Alg. de Lie}}(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h})\) at \(\operatorname{Lie}(u)\) is identified with \(\mathrm{Z}^1(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h})\). We must therefore prove that the canonical map \(\mathrm{Z}^1(G, \mathfrak{h}) \to \mathrm{Z}^1(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h})\) is bijective. But \(\mathrm{H}^1(G, \mathfrak{h}) = \mathrm{H}^1(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}) = 0\) (7.3.2 and 7.3.3) and this map is identified with the obvious map \[ \mathfrak{h}/\mathrm{H}^0(G, \mathfrak{h}) \longrightarrow \mathfrak{h}/\mathrm{H}^0(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}), \] and one concludes by 7.3.2.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.3.6

It is plausible that if \(S\) is a locally noetherian prescheme, \(G\) a simply connected semi-simple \(S\)-group, \(H\) a smooth \(S\)-group prescheme, \(\widehat{G}\) and \(\widehat{H}\) their formal completions along the unit section, every homomorphism from \(\widehat{G}\) into \(\widehat{H}\) comes from a unique homomorphism from \(G\) into \(H\), which would generalize 7.3.1 (iii). When \(S\) is the spectrum of a field and \(H\) is affine and of finite type, this follows from a theorem of Dieudonné (Lie groups and Lie hyperalgebras…, VI, Am. J. of Maths, 1957, p. 369, th. 4). One will note however that, if \(S\) is not of characteristic zero, the preceding conjecture becomes false if one drops the hypothesis that \(S\) is locally noetherian (for otherwise one would deduce that \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, H)\) would always be affine over \(S\), which is not the case, as we shall see in 7.4 below).
7.4. An example
By way of example, we shall determine \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S},\ \mathrm{SL}_{2,S}). \]

Recall (Exp. XX, no 5) that \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\) is the \(S\)-group scheme formed by the matrices \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) over \(S\) satisfying \(ad - bc = 1\). A maximal torus \(T\) is defined by the monomorphism \(\alpha^* : \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \to \mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\) \[ \alpha^*(z) = \begin{pmatrix} z & 0\\ 0 & z^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \] A root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) is defined by \(\alpha(\alpha^*(z)) = z^2\), a corresponding monomorphism \[ p : \mathbf{G}_{a,S} \longrightarrow \mathrm{SL}_{2,S} \] being defined by \[ p(x) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Finally, the representative of the Weyl group corresponding to \(u = p(1)\) is \[ w = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \] Recall on the other hand (Exp. XX, 6.2) that \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\) is generated by \(T\), \(p(\mathbf{G}_{a,S})\) and \(w\), subject to the relations \[ \begin{aligned} \alpha^*(z)\, p(x)\, \alpha^*(z^{-1}) &= p(z^2 x),\\ w\, \alpha^*(z)\, w^{-1} &= \alpha^*(z^{-1}),\\ w^2 &= \alpha^*(-1),\\ (wu)^3 &= 1. \end{aligned} \]

Let \(f\) be an endomorphism of \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\). It first of all defines a homomorphism \(f \circ \alpha^* : \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \to \mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\). The kernel \(\operatorname{Ker}(f \circ \alpha^*)\) is a closed subgroup of \(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}\), hence is locally over \(S\) equal to a \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n,S}\) (\(n \geqslant 1\)) or to \(\mathbf{G}_{m,S}\). After possibly shrinking \(S\), we may therefore assume that there exist an \(n \in \mathbf{N}\) and a monomorphism \[ f' : \mathbf{G}_{m,S} \longrightarrow \mathrm{SL}_{2,S} \] such that \(f \circ \alpha^*(z) = f'(z^n)\).

By virtue of the conjugacy of the monomorphisms \(\mathbf{G}_{m,S} \to \mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\), one may, after a covering extension for (ét) of the base, find a section \(g\) of \(G\) such that \(f \circ \alpha^*(z) = \operatorname{int}(g) \circ \alpha^*(z^n)\). Transforming \(f\) by \(\operatorname{int}(g)\), we are thus reduced to the case where there exists an \(n \in \mathbf{N}\) such that \(f \circ \alpha^*(z) = \alpha^*(z^n)\).

Let us now consider the morphism \[ f \circ p : \mathbf{G}_{a,S} \longrightarrow \mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\,. \] It satisfies the condition \[ \alpha^*(z^n)(f \circ p)(x)\alpha^*(s^n)^{-1} = (f \circ p)(z^2 x). \] If \(n = 0\), it follows at once that \(f \circ p\) is invariant under the homotheties of \(\mathbf{G}_{a,S}\), hence constant. If \(n \ne 0\), we may apply Exp. XXII, 4.1.9; \(x \mapsto x^n\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathbf{G}_{a,S}\), and there exists a \(\lambda \in \mathbf{G}_{m,S}\) such that \[ f \circ p(x) = p(\lambda x^n); \] this relation is moreover valid for \(n = 0\), on taking \(\lambda = 1\). After possibly extending \(S\) once again, we can find a \(z \in \mathbf{G}_{m,S}\) with \(z^2 = \lambda\). Replacing \(f\) by \(\operatorname{int}(\alpha^*(z)) \circ f\), we are thus reduced to the case where one has \[ f \circ \alpha^*(z) = \alpha^*(z^n), \qquad f \circ p(x) = p(x^n). \]

Finally, one must have \(f(w)\alpha^*(z^n)f(w)^{-1} = \alpha^*(z^n)^{-1}\) and \((f(w)u)^3 = 1\). By virtue of Exp. XX, 3.8, this entails \(f(w) = w^n\). Since \(G\) is generated by \(T\), \(p(\mathbf{G}_{a,S})\) and \(w\), this entails that for every \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{smallmatrix}\right) \in G(S')\), \(S' \to S\), one has \[ f \begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a^n & b^n\\ c^n & d^n \end{pmatrix}. \]

Summarising the preceding discussion, one sees that locally on \(S\) for the étale topology, one can find, for every endomorphism \(f\) of \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\), an (inner) automorphism \(\varphi\) of \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\) and an integer \(n \geqslant 0\) such that \(f = \varphi \circ \mathrm{F}_n\), where \[ \mathrm{F}_n \begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a^n & b^n\\ c^n & d^n \end{pmatrix}. \] Let us remark that if \(f = \varphi \circ \mathrm{F}_n\), the integer \(n\) is completely determined by a fibre \(f_s\) of \(f\), for example by \(\operatorname{Ker}(f_s)\). It follows that \(n\) is a locally constant function on \(S\).

One deduces at once that if \(f\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S}\), then \(S\) decomposes canonically into a sum of open and closed sub-preschemes \(S_0\), \(S_1\), \(S_{p^n}\) (where \(p^n\) runs through the set of powers \(> 0\) of the prime numbers) such that:
(i) \(f_{S_0}\) is the zero morphism,
(ii) \(f_{S_1}\) is an isomorphism (= an inner automorphism),

(iii) \(S_{p^n}\) is of characteristic \(p\), and \(f_{S_{p^n}}\) decomposes in a unique way in the form \(\varphi \circ \mathrm{F}_p^n\), where \(\varphi\) is an inner automorphism and \(\mathrm{F}_p\) the Frobenius endomorphism of \(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{F}_p}\).
In other words, \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathbf{Z}\text{-gr.}}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{Z}},\ \mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{Z}})\) is the sum prescheme:
(i) of a scheme isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbf{Z})\),
(ii) of a scheme isomorphic to \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathbf{Z}\text{-gr.}}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{Z}}) \simeq \operatorname{ad}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{Z}})\),

(iii) for each number \(p\) and each integer \(> 0\), of a scheme isomorphic to \(\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathbf{F}_p\text{-gr.}}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{F}_p}) \simeq \operatorname{ad}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{F}_p})\).
It follows in particular that
(i) \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathbf{F}_p\text{-gr.}}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{F}_p},\ \mathrm{SL}_{2,\mathbf{F}_p})\) has an infinite number of connected components, and hence is not quasi-compact.
(ii) If \(S\) is a scheme of unequal characteristics, \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathrm{SL}_{2,S},\ \mathrm{SL}_{2,S})\) is not flat over \(S\).

pages.title: 8. Appendix: Cohomology of a smooth group over a henselian ring. Cohomology and the functor \(\prod\)

blocks.html: 8. Appendix: Cohomology of a smooth group over a henselian ring. Cohomology and the functor \(\prod\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1

Let \(S\) be a henselian local scheme, \(s\) its closed point, \(G\) a smooth \(S\)-group scheme such that every finite subset of \(G\) is contained in an affine open set (*). Then

(i) If \(P\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\), there exists a finite surjective étale \(S' \to S\) which trivialises \(P\). One has \(\operatorname{Fib}(S, H) \simeq \mathrm{H}^1_{\text{ét}}(S, H)\).

(ii) For every finite surjective étale morphism \(S' \to S\), the canonical map \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S' \otimes_S k(s)/k(s), G_s) \] is bijective.

(iii) The canonical map \[ \operatorname{Fib}(S, G) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Fib}(k(s), G_s) \] is bijective.
(*) This last condition is in fact unnecessary (cf. Grothendieck, Groupe de Brauer III, in Dix Exposés sur la cohomologie des schémas, North-Holland, 1968, theorem 11.7 and remarks 11.8.3).

If \(K\) is a finite separable extension of \(k(s)\), there exists a finite surjective étale \(S' \to S\) such that \(K \simeq S' \otimes_S k(s)\). If \(P\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\), then \(P\) is smooth over \(S\), hence \(P_s\) is smooth over \(k(s)\); there therefore exists a finite separable extension \(K\) of \(k(s)\) such that \(P_K\) possesses a section. Representing \(K\) as was said above, one sees that \(P_{S'}\) possesses a section by "Hensel's lemma", which proves the first part of (i).

Conversely, if \(P\) is a principal homogeneous sheaf under \(G\) for the étale topology, there exists a finite surjective étale \(S' \to S\) which trivialises \(P\) (indeed every covering family of a henselian local scheme for the étale topology is dominated by a family reduced to a single morphism \(S' \to S\) of the desired form).

By virtue of the descent hypothesis made on \(G\), \(P\) is representable (SGA 1, VIII, 7.6), which completes the proof of (i), and shows that (ii) implies (iii). It therefore only remains for us to prove (ii).

The map in (ii) is injective: let \(P\) and \(\mathrm{Q}\) be two principal homogeneous bundles under \(G\) trivialised by \(S'\). Consider the \(S\)-group sheaf \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{G\text{-fibrés}}(P, \mathrm{Q})\); since \(H_{S'}\) is isomorphic to \(G_{S'}\), \(H\) is representable, by virtue of the second hypothesis on \(G\), cf. above. If \(H(k(s)) \ne \varnothing\), then \(H(S) \ne \varnothing\) by Hensel's lemma, hence \(P\) and \(\mathrm{Q}\) are isomorphic.

Let us finally prove that the map in (ii) is surjective, or again that the canonical map \[ \mathrm{Z}^1(S'/S, G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Z}^1(S' \otimes_S k(s)/k(s), G_s) \] is surjective. Let \(\mathbf{Z}^1\) be the \(S\)-functor defined by \[ \mathbf{Z}^1(T) = \mathrm{Z}^1(S' \times_S T/T, G_T); \] the preceding map is identified with the map \[ \mathbf{Z}^1(S') \longrightarrow \mathbf{Z}^1(S' \otimes_S k(s)); \] by a further application of Hensel's lemma, it suffices to prove that \(\mathbf{Z}^1\) is representable by a smooth \(S\)-prescheme.

Let us prove that \(\mathbf{Z}^1\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme locally of finite presentation. Let \(\mathbf{C}^i\), \(i = 0, 1, \ldots\), be the \(S\)-functor defined by \[ \mathbf{C}^i(T) = \mathrm{C}^i(S' \times_S T/T, G_T), \] that is to say \[ \mathbf{C}^i(T) = G((S' \times_S T/T)^{i+1}) = G((S'/S)^{i+1} \times_S T), \] or again \[ \mathbf{C}^i = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_S((S'/S)^{i+1}, G). \] Since \(\mathbf{Z}^1\) is obtained from \(\mathbf{C}^1\) and \(\mathbf{C}^2\) by fibre products, it suffices to prove that \(\mathbf{C}^i\), \(i = 1, 2\), is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme locally of finite presentation.

If \(T \to S\) is a finite surjective étale morphism which decomposes \(S'\), then \[ \mathbf{C}^i \times_S T = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_T((S' \times_S T/T)^{i+1}, G_T) \] is representable by a product of \(n\) copies of \(G_T\), where \(n\) is the degree of \((S'/S)^{i+1}\). Applying once again the hypothesis on \(G\), one deduces that \(\mathbf{C}^i\) is indeed representable by an \(S\)-prescheme locally of finite presentation (SGA 1, VIII, loc. cit.).

To prove that \(\mathbf{Z}^1\) is smooth, we must now, by definition, prove that if \(T\) is an affine \(S\)-scheme and \(T_0\) the closed sub-prescheme defined by the Ideal \(\mathscr{J}\) of square zero, the canonical map \[ \mathbf{Z}^1(T) \longrightarrow \mathbf{Z}^1(T_0) \] is surjective. Since \(G\) is smooth, the canonical map \(G(T) \to G(T_0)\) is surjective, and it suffices to prove that the canonical map \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S' \times_S T/T, G_T) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S' \times_S T_0/T_0, G_{T_0}) \] is bijective.
Changing notation slightly and generalising the hypotheses, it now suffices for us to prove:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.1.8

Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be two affine schemes, \(S' \to S\) a faithfully flat morphism, \(\mathscr{J}\) an Ideal of square zero on \(S\), \(S_0\) the closed sub-prescheme which it defines, \(G\) a smooth \(S\)-group. Put \(S'_0 = S' \times_S S_0\), \(G_0 = G \times_S S_0\). The canonical map \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S'_0/S_0, G_0) \] is bijective.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 8.1.9

If \(G\) is assumed commutative, the same assertion holds for all the \(\mathrm{H}^i\), \(i > 0\), with an analogous proof.

Let \(\mathscr{M}_0\) be the quasi-coherent \(\mathscr{O}_{S_0}\)-Module \[ \mathscr{M}_0 = \operatorname{Lie}(G_0/S_0) \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{S_0}} \mathscr{J}\,. \] For each \(S_0\)-prescheme \(T_0\) (resp. each \(S\)-prescheme \(T\)), put \[ \mathrm{M}_0(T_0) = \mathrm{H}^0(T_0, \mathscr{M}_0 \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{S_0}} \mathscr{O}_{T_0}), \] (resp. \(\mathrm{M}(T) = \mathrm{M}_0(T_0)\). On the other hand, let \(\overline{G} = \prod_{S/S_0} G_0\) be the \(S\)-group functor defined by \(\overline{G}(T) = G_0(T_0)\). It is known (Exp. III, no 0) that for every affine \(S\)-scheme \(T\) there exists an exact sequence, functorial in \(T\): \[ 1 \longrightarrow \mathrm{M}(T) \longrightarrow G(T) \longrightarrow \overline{G}(T) \longrightarrow 1 \] We have to study the map \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S'_0/S_0, G_0) = \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \overline{G}). \] Let us first suppose \(G\) commutative. One then has an exact cohomology sequence \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \mathrm{M}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \overline{G}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^2(S'/S, \mathrm{M}); \] but \[ \mathrm{H}^i(S'/S, \mathrm{M}) = \mathrm{H}^i(S'_0/S_0, \mathrm{M}_0) = \mathrm{H}^i(S'_0/S_0, \mathscr{M}_0), \] and it is known (TDTE II, B, Lemma 1.1) that \(\mathrm{H}^i(S'_0/S_0, \mathscr{M}_0) = 0\) for \(i \ne 0\).

If now \(G\) is not commutative, we must use the exact sequence of non-abelian cohomology. If \(u \in \mathrm{Z}^1(S'/S, G)\), it is known that the elements of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G)\) which have the same image in \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \overline{G})\) as the class of \(u\) lie in the image of the corresponding coboundary map: \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \mathrm{M}_u) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G), \] where \(\mathrm{M}_u\) is the \(S\)-functor \(\mathrm{M}\) "twisted by \(u\)". Likewise, if \(v\) is an element of \(\mathrm{Z}^1(S'/S, \overline{G})\), there exists a "coboundary" \[ \Delta(v) \in \mathrm{H}^2(S'/S, \mathrm{M}_v), \] where \(\mathrm{M}_v\) is the \(S\)-functor \(\mathrm{M}\) "twisted by \(v\)", such that \(\Delta(v) = 0\) if and only if the class of \(v\) lies in the image of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, G)\). It suffices for us to prove that one has \(\mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \mathrm{M}_u) = \mathrm{H}^2(S'/S, \mathrm{M}_v) = 0\).

Now let us recall (Exp III, no 0) that the action of \(\overline{G}\) on \(\mathrm{M}\) defined by the exact sequence is none other than the one deduced functorially from the adjoint representation of \(G_0\): \[ \operatorname{ad} : G_0 \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}_{\mathscr{O}_{S_0}}(\operatorname{Lie}(G_0/S_0)). \] The element \(u\) (resp. \(v\)) therefore acts on \(\mathrm{M}_{S' \times_S S'}\) by means of an \(S'_0 \times_{S_0} S'_0\)-automorphism of \(\operatorname{Lie}(G_0/S_0)\). Since \(u\) (resp. \(v\)) is a cocycle, this automorphism is a descent datum; let \(\mathscr{L}_u\) (resp. \(\mathscr{L}_v\)) denote the quasi-coherent \(\mathscr{O}_{S_0}\)-Module so obtained. One checks at once that for \(T \to S\) one has \[ \mathrm{M}_u(T) = \mathrm{H}^0(T_0, \mathscr{L}_u \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{S_0}} \mathscr{J} \otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{S_0}} \mathscr{O}_{T_0}) \] and the same relation on replacing \(u\) by \(v\). One therefore has \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{H}^1(S'/S, \mathrm{M}_u) &= \mathrm{H}^1(S'_0/S_0, \mathscr{L}_u \otimes \mathscr{J})\\ \mathrm{H}^2(S'/S, \mathrm{M}_v) &= \mathrm{H}^2(S'_0/S_0, \mathscr{L}_v \otimes \mathscr{J}), \end{aligned} \] and both are indeed zero by virtue of the result already used.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.2

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a category possessing fibre products, equipped with a topology coarser than the canonical topology, \(S' \to S\) a morphism of \(\mathscr{C}\), \(G'\) an \(S'\)-group sheaf, \(G\) the \(S\)-group sheaf \(\prod_{S'/S} G'\). Let \(\mathrm{H}^1_S(S', G') \subset \mathrm{H}^1(S', G')\) be the set of classes of principal homogeneous sheaves under \(G'\) which are trivialised by a sieve of \(S'\) obtained by base change from a suitable covering sieve of \(S\). The canonical map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G) \to \mathrm{H}^1(S', G')\) defined by the functor \[ P \longmapsto P \times_S S' \] induces a bijection \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{H}^1_S(S', G'); \] the inverse bijection is defined by the functor \(P' \mapsto \prod_{S'/S} P'\).

For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{C}_{/S}\), one has by definition an isomorphism functorial in \(X\) \[ \operatorname{Hom}_S(X, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Hom}_{S'}(X \times_S S', G'). \] One therefore has, for each \(S\)-object \(T\), a bijection functorial in \(T\) \[ \mathrm{H}^1(T/S, G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{H}^1(T'/S', G'). \] Replacing now the single morphism \(T \to S\) by an arbitrary covering family of \(S\) and passing to the inductive limit, one deduces the first part of the statement. The second part follows from it without difficulty.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.3

Under the conditions of 8.2, the assertion \(\mathrm{H}^1_S(S', G') = \mathrm{H}^1(S', G')\) is local on \(S\): suppose that there exists a covering family \(\{S_i \to S\}\) such that for every \(i\) one has \(\mathrm{H}^1_{S_i}(S' \times_S S_i, G') = \mathrm{H}^1(S' \times_S S_i, G')\). Then \(\mathrm{H}^1_S(S', G') = \mathrm{H}^1(S', G')\).

Indeed, let \(P'\) be a principal homogeneous sheaf under \(G'\). For every \(i\), put \(P'_i = P \times_{S'} (S' \times_S S_i)\); by virtue of the hypothesis, there exists a covering family \(\{S_{ij} \to S_i\}\) such that for each \(j\), \(P' \times_{S'} (S' \times_S S_{ij})\) possesses a section. But \(\{S_{ij} \to S\}\) is a covering family of \(S\), and \(P'\) is indeed trivialised by the covering family of \(S'\) obtained from the latter by base change.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.4

Let \(S' \to S\) be a finite étale morphism of preschemes. Let \(G'\) be an \(S'\)-group sheaf, \(G\) the \(S\)-group sheaf \(\prod_{S'/S} G'\). For the étale topology (resp. the finite local étale topology, resp. (fpqc)), the functors \[ \begin{aligned} P &\longmapsto P \times_S S'\\ P' &\longmapsto \textstyle\prod_{S'/S} P' \end{aligned} \] induce bijections inverse to one another: \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, G) \simeq \mathrm{H}^1(S', G'). \]

By 8.2, it suffices to show that \(\mathrm{H}^1_S(S', G') = \mathrm{H}^1(S', G')\). By 8.3, it suffices to do so locally for the finite local étale topology; one may therefore suppose that \(S'\) is a finite direct sum of copies of \(S\), say \(\mathrm{I}_S\), where \(\mathrm{I}\) is a suitable finite set. Then \(G'\) is given by a family \((G_i)_{i \in \mathrm{I}}\) of sheaves on \(S\) and \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S', G') \simeq \prod_{i \in \mathrm{I}} \mathrm{H}^1(S, G_i). \] On the other hand \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, G) \simeq \prod_{i \in \mathrm{I}} \mathrm{H}^1(S, G_i), \] whence, by virtue of 8.2, \(\mathrm{H}^1_S(S', G') = \mathrm{H}^1(S', G')\). Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 8.5

One may interpret 8.2 and 8.3 by means of the following exact sequence (\(f\) is the given morphism \(S' \to S\)) \[ 1 \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S, f_*(G')) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S', G') \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^0(S, \mathrm{R}^1 f_*(G')). \] In the commutative case, this exact sequence follows from the Leray spectral sequence; it is still valid in the non-commutative case (cf. Giraud's Thesis).

In this form, one sees that the result is still valid if \(f\) is only assumed finite, or simply integral, the topology being the étale topology, for one has, for every \(G'\), \[ \mathrm{R}^1 f_*(G') = \text{final sheaf}, \] by virtue of SGA 4, VIII, 5.3.

On the other hand, this result becomes false if one takes a topology such as (fpqc) or (fppf), even if \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(k\) an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p \ne 0\), \(S' = \operatorname{Spec}(k[t]/t^2)\), \(G' = \boldsymbol{\mu}_p\) or \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_p\).

Likewise, 8.2 becomes false, even for the étale topology, if one deletes from it the hypothesis that \(f\) is finite, as one sees by taking for \(f\) an open immersion; for example if \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(V)\), \(V\) a complete discrete valuation ring with algebraically closed residue field, \(S'\) being the open subset induced at the generic point, and \(G'\) the constant group \((\mathbf{Z}/n\mathbf{Z})_{S'}\), with \(n\) prime to the residue characteristic of \(V\), one has \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G) = 0\), \(\mathrm{H}^1(S', G') \ne 0\). Replacing moreover \(S'\) by \(S \amalg S'\), one deduces an analogous example, with \(S' \to S\) étale surjective, hence covering for the topology under consideration.
